title: Why Generation Speed Doesn't Shorten the Job
description: Where the hours actually go on an AI-assisted change, and why a five-minute generation and a five-hour job are not in tension.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which parts of a change AI generation actually shortens
Distinguish generation time from the review and integration time that replaces it

contentSections.title: The five minutes everyone remembers

contentSections.body:
A contractor tells a client the invoice for a feature is nine hours. The client has watched the tool generate the whole thing in about ninety seconds, on a screen-share, three days earlier. "Ninety seconds," the client says. "Nine hours for what?"

The contractor isn't padding the invoice. The ninety seconds and the nine hours are both real, and they're not measuring the same thing.

contentSections.scenario: A mid-sized feature — add a discount-code field to checkout, including validation, an audit log entry, and a test suite — goes through an AI-assisted build. The tool generates a full working diff in under two minutes. The developer then spends: 40 minutes reading every line against the discount rules doc, 25 minutes finding and fixing a bug in how percentage-off stacks with a prior promo, 90 minutes writing three edge-case tests the generated suite missed, 20 minutes rewording the audit log message so it matches the format finance actually parses, and 15 minutes on PR description and a walkthrough for the reviewer.
contentSections.question: Which part of that timeline did the tool actually shorten?

options.label: All of it — the whole feature took under three hours instead of nine
Only the two minutes of generation; the other three hours and ten minutes are unchanged by the tool being fast
Nothing — the total time is the same either way

feedback.all: It feels that way because the two minutes is the part you watched happen fast. But writing that discount-code feature by hand, a competent developer would have spent maybe 90 minutes typing it — not three hours and ten minutes. The tool didn't compress the reading, the bug-hunting, the missing tests, or the audit-log correction. Those took as long as they take.
feedback.gen_only: Right. The tool replaced roughly ninety minutes of typing with two minutes of generation — a real saving, just a smaller one than it looks like. Everything after generation is work a careful developer would do at close to the same speed whether the diff came from typing or from a prompt, because reading, verifying, and testing don't get faster just because writing did.
feedback.nothing: The generation step itself genuinely is close to free — two minutes instead of what would have been well over an hour of typing. The saving is real. It's just concentrated in one part of the job, and it's the smallest part.

contentSections.concept: **Generation speed shortens generation. It does not shorten verification.** A change has always had a typing cost and a thinking-and-checking cost, and the two were never equal — even before any of this, senior developers spent more time reading and reviewing than typing. AI tooling collapses the typing cost toward zero. It does nothing to the review cost, because review time is set by how much you need to trust the result, not by how the result was produced.

contentSections.body:
This is the single most common estimating mistake on AI-assisted work, in both directions. Estimate the way you used to — hours roughly proportional to how much code will exist — and you'll overshoot on generation-heavy, review-light work like scaffolding a new CRUD endpoint from a clear spec. Estimate as if the tool being fast makes *everything* fast, and you'll blow every estimate that has real review weight in it: unfamiliar code, ambiguous requirements, anything security- or money-adjacent.

The fix isn't a different multiplier. It's estimating the two costs separately, because they no longer move together.
Generation got cheap. Verification didn't. An estimate that doesn't separate the two is a guess wearing a number.

contentSections.title: Where the old shortcuts stop working

contentSections.body: "How long will this take?" used to have a rough shortcut: look at how much code the change probably needs, divide by how fast you type and think at once. That shortcut isn't wrong now. It's answering a question nobody's asking anymore.

contentSections.scenario: A team lead keeps underestimating AI-assisted tickets by roughly the same margin — not wildly, just consistently short by 30–40%. Every ticket, on every project, for two months.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism behind a consistent, similar-sized miss across many different tickets?

options.label: The team is bad at estimating and needs training
The estimate is still built on a typing-time model, and typing time is no longer the dominant cost
The AI tool is unreliable and generates broken code

feedback.training: A consistent, similarly-sized miss across many different kinds of tickets isn't what a skills gap looks like — a skills gap produces noisy, ticket-specific misses. A steady miss points at the estimating *model* itself, not the people running it.
feedback.model: This is the pattern to recognize: a systematic underestimate of roughly the same size, ticket after ticket, is what you get when the estimating formula hasn't updated even though the work has. If "how much code" used to predict "how long," and generation removed most of the typing time, the formula now silently omits the biggest remaining cost — review — and it will miss by about the same amount every time, because review is proportionally about the same share of every ticket.
feedback.tool: If the tool were unreliable, the misses would track with how much was generated — bigger generations, bigger misses — and would vary a lot by task. A steady, similarly-sized gap across different tickets points at something structural in the estimate itself, not at the tool's reliability on any one of them.

contentSections.mechanism: **The old shortcut assumed typing time and thinking time moved together, because for decades they roughly did.** AI generation broke that coupling in one direction only — it cut typing, and left thinking, verifying and integrating alone. Any estimating habit built on the old coupling will now under-predict by close to a fixed proportion, because it's silently still charging for typing time that mostly isn't being spent, while charging nothing extra for the review time that took its place.

contentSections.body: A steady, similarly-sized miss on every estimate is a sign the formula is wrong, not that you keep getting unlucky.

title: Estimating Review, Not Typing
description: A procedure for estimating the part of the job that now takes the time: reading, verifying, testing and integrating a generated change.

learningObjectives.text: Break a brief into the review sub-costs that actually consume time
Produce an estimate that accounts for review as its own line item

contentSections.title: Naming the review costs

contentSections.body: "Add pagination to the orders list" sounds like a ninety-minute ticket, and the generated diff arrives in ninety seconds, complete-looking. Then someone has to actually believe it's correct — and that belief is the expensive part now.

contentSections.problem: Estimate: "Add pagination to the orders list endpoint, 50 items per page, matching the pattern already used on the invoices endpoint." You have access to an AI coding tool. Produce a time estimate with its parts shown, not just a total.

steps.label: Estimate generation time
steps.work: Near-zero as a distinct cost — call it 5 minutes for the prompt, the review of the first draft, and one or two follow-up prompts to fix an obvious miss.
steps.why: This is the part that used to dominate and now doesn't. Naming it small, explicitly, is what stops the rest of the estimate from quietly inheriting an old typing-time assumption.

steps.label: Estimate correctness review
steps.work: 20 minutes: read the generated diff against the invoices pattern it's supposed to match, check the SQL for an off-by-one on page boundaries (a known failure mode for this exact task), confirm the total-count query isn't re-running the full unpaginated query underneath.
steps.why: This is where an estimate has to be concrete about *what could be wrong*, not just "review the code." Pagination has two or three specific, well-known failure modes — naming them is what makes the 20 minutes defensible rather than a round number.

steps.label: Estimate test-writing
steps.work: 25 minutes: the generated tests probably cover the happy path (page 2 of 5) but need edge cases added by hand — page 0 or negative, page past the last page, page size larger than total records, and an empty result set.
steps.why: Generated test suites are reliably strong on the case the prompt described and reliably weak on the cases it didn't think to ask for. Budgeting for the edge cases as a separate line, rather than assuming the generated suite is done, is what keeps this from becoming the thing that blows the estimate.

steps.label: Estimate integration and PR overhead
steps.work: 15 minutes: rebase against the invoices endpoint if it's moved since, write a PR description explaining the pattern match, and one round of addressing reviewer comments.
steps.why: This cost exists whether the code was typed or generated, and estimators forget it precisely because it feels like it belongs to "before," not to this ticket.

steps.label: Total and sanity-check
steps.work: 5 + 20 + 25 + 15 = 65 minutes, call it 70 with a small buffer. Compare against gut feel: does an hour and ten minutes feel right for a well-understood, pattern-matched change with known edge cases? Yes — it's small precisely because the pattern already exists and the failure modes are known in advance.
steps.why: The sanity check isn't decorative. An estimate built from parts can still be wrong if one part was guessed badly — comparing the total against intuition catches a part that's quietly off by 3x.

faded.problem: Now estimate: "Add a CSV export button to the orders list, using the same export library already used on the invoices page, output the same eight columns as the on-screen table." Same tool, same context.

blanks.prompt: Generation time — in minutes
blanks.why: A pattern-matched, well-specified change generates fast and close to right on the first pass — this is structurally the same shape as the pagination example.

blanks.prompt: What's the single most likely correctness bug to check for in a generated CSV export?
blanks.answer: column order or a missing column doesn't match the on-screen table
blanks.why: CSV export bugs are almost always a mismatch between what's displayed and what's exported — a column renamed on screen but not in the export mapping, or a computed column left out because it isn't a raw database field.

blanks.prompt: Name one edge case a generated test suite is likely to miss here.
blanks.answer: an empty orders list, or a field containing a comma or quote that needs CSV escaping
blanks.why: CSV escaping is a classic generated-suite gap — the happy-path test uses clean sample data that never contains the character that breaks a naive export.

blanks.prompt: Roughly what should the total estimate be — in minutes, one number
blanks.why: Smaller than the pagination task: one clear failure mode instead of three, a smaller and more obvious edge-case set, and a library already proven on the invoices page. The estimate should be visibly smaller, and be able to say why.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the review sub-costs — correctness check, test-writing, integration — as separate lines, each tied to a specific thing that could be wrong, before adding them up.** A total with no named parts is a guess with a decimal point. A total built from named, checkable parts is an estimate you can defend, and re-check, when it's wrong.

contentSections.body: Estimate correctness review, test-writing and integration as their own named lines. A total with no parts is not an estimate.

contentSections.title: Sizing review time when you don't know the code yet

contentSections.body: The pagination and CSV examples both had something in common: familiar code, a clear pattern to match. Most tickets aren't that generous.

contentSections.scenario: A ticket asks you to add rate-limiting to a public API endpoint in a codebase you've never worked in before. You don't yet know the existing auth middleware, whether there's already a rate-limit library in use, or how errors are surfaced to API consumers. The generated diff takes four minutes to produce and looks plausible on a skim.
contentSections.question: Before reading the codebase at all, what's a reasonable estimate — in minutes — for correctness review alone (not test-writing, not integration) on unfamiliar, security-adjacent code like this?
contentSections.explanation: Somewhere around an hour is realistic, and the reason is worth saying out loud: unfamiliarity and consequence both push review time up independently. You can't verify "does this match the existing pattern" when you don't know the existing pattern yet — so part of the 60 minutes is just learning the codebase enough to review against it. And rate-limiting on a public endpoint is the kind of change where getting it wrong is either a security hole (limit too loose) or an outage (limit too tight, or applied to the wrong key) — consequence that size buys a slower, more skeptical read regardless of how good the generated code looks on first glance. A four-minute-old, plausible-looking diff on unfamiliar, high-consequence code is exactly the situation where trusting the skim is how the 60 minutes gets skipped and the incident happens instead.

contentSections.body:
Two variables move review time independently of how much code exists: **how familiar you are with what's being touched**, and **how much it costs if you're wrong**. A one-line change to an unfamiliar payments function can rightly take longer to review than a fifty-line change to a page you wrote last week. Estimating by lines of generated code, or even by feature size, misses both.

A usable shortcut: ask two questions before estimating review time. *Do I already know this code well enough to spot something subtly off?* If not, add time to learn it — that's real review cost, not overhead. *What does it cost if this is wrong and ships anyway?* Scale review time to that, not to how confident the diff looks.
Review time scales with unfamiliarity and consequence, not with how much code was generated or how confident it looks.

title: The Unknowns That Make an Estimate a Guess, Said Out Loud
description: Naming the specific unknowns in a brief — not hedging generally, but listing what you don't yet know and what it would cost if the answer is bad.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific unknowns hiding inside a scoping request
State an unknown's cost rather than burying it in a padded estimate

contentSections.title: Padding is a worse answer than naming

contentSections.body: Two developers get the same vague brief: "integrate our product with the client's inventory system, they'll send API docs." One quotes three days. The other quotes "one day if their API is what the docs say, four if it isn't — and I won't know which until I've read their docs, which I haven't seen yet." Only one of those is honest about what's actually known.

contentSections.scenario: You're scoping: "Add a Slack notification when an order over $500 fails payment." Before writing a number, you list what you don't yet know.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real unknowns worth naming before estimating — not just things to figure out while coding?

items.label: Whether the team already has a Slack webhook configured for this workspace, or one needs to be created and approved
Whether "over $500" means the order total or the failed-payment amount specifically (they can differ with partial payments)
Whether a payment that fails then succeeds on retry within the same session should still notify
The exact Slack SDK method name for sending a message
What color the Slack message's sidebar accent should be

explanation.webhook: This one can add a day by itself if a new webhook needs security review and approval — and it's knowable before you start, just by asking. That makes it an unknown worth naming, not a coding detail to discover mid-task.
explanation.threshold: This changes what code you write, not just how you write it. If it means failed-payment amount and partial payments are common, that's a different condition than a flat order-total check. Worth one question before starting, not a guess baked into the estimate.
explanation.retry: A genuine business-logic ambiguity that changes correct behavior, not implementation detail — notifying on every transient failure during a retry storm is a very different system than notifying once per genuinely failed order.
explanation.syntax: This is exactly the kind of thing generation handles well and doesn't belong in a scoping conversation — it costs seconds to look up or generate correctly, not a decision anyone needs to make in advance.
explanation.color: A cosmetic default exists or can be picked in five seconds; it doesn't change scope and doesn't warrant flagging as an unknown.

contentSections.synthesis: **An unknown worth naming is one that changes either the estimate or the correct behavior of the thing you'd build — not one that changes how you'd type it.** The webhook question can cost a day. The Slack SDK method name costs a search. Sorting a brief into those two piles before estimating is the actual skill; everything that lands in the second pile just gets built.

contentSections.body: The instinct under pressure is to fold unknowns into a bigger number and say nothing — quote three days instead of one, so there's room if the API docs turn out to be wrong. This protects the estimate and nobody else. The client can't decide whether the risk is worth de-risking first (a half-day spike reading their docs before committing to a number) because they were never told there *was* a risk. Naming the unknown and its cost turns a private hedge into a decision the client gets to make.
An unknown that changes scope or correctness belongs in the estimate by name, with its cost — not folded silently into a bigger number.

contentSections.title: Saying it out loud

contentSections.body: "It depends" is true and useless. "It's one day if X, three if not X, and I'll know by Tuesday" is the same honesty with a decision attached to it.

contentSections.code:
Estimate for: "Migrate the reporting dashboard to pull from the new analytics warehouse instead of the old one."

Quote sent to client: “5–7 business days.”
contentSections.question: What's missing that makes this quote worse than useless — worse than just being imprecise?

options.label: It doesn't say which of the two numbers, 5 or 7, is more likely
It doesn't name what the 2-day range depends on, so the client can't do anything with the uncertainty
It should be a single number, not a range, because ranges look unprofessional

feedback.which: A midpoint or a most-likely number would help a little, but it's not the main problem — even a precise "6 days" would still leave the client unable to do anything about the two-day swing, because they still wouldn't know what causes it.
feedback.why: Right. A range with no named cause is not more honest than a single number — it's the same guess with a hedge stapled on. The client can't ask "can we find out sooner whether it's the 5-day version or the 7-day version?" because nothing tells them what the two-day gap is *about*. A range is only useful information if it comes with the variable that moves it.
feedback.range: Ranges are completely normal and often more honest than a single number — the problem here isn't that it's a range, it's that the range is unexplained. “5 days if the warehouse schema matches the old one's column names, 7 if we need a mapping layer, and I'll know which by end of day tomorrow” is a range doing its job.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A range with no named variable protects the estimator and informs nobody. The fix costs one sentence: name the specific thing the range depends on, and, if possible, when you'll know which side of it you're on. That turns “we don't know yet” from an ending into a plan — the client learns there's a fast, cheap way to collapse the uncertainty (check the schema first) instead of just being told to expect anywhere from five to seven days and find out later.

contentSections.body: A range is only honest if it names what moves it. “5–7 days” says nothing; “5 days if the schema matches, 7 if not” is a decision the client can act on.

title: Scoping Around a Variable-Capacity Week
description: Turning a task estimate into a realistic week, when the number of hours you can actually work varies and you don't always know in advance which kind of day you'll get.

learningObjectives.text: Build a scope and delivery plan that accounts for variable daily capacity
Structure deliverables so a bad day doesn't block the whole commitment

contentSections.title: A week is not five identical days

contentSections.body: "I have a good week, most weeks" is true and it's the wrong unit. A client doesn't experience your average; they experience Tuesday, specifically, when Tuesday is a crash day and the deliverable was due Wednesday morning.

contentSections.scenario: A developer estimates a task at 20 hours of focused work. They plan to deliver it inside a five-day week, working what they call “a normal day” each day.
contentSections.question: If roughly one day in five is a low-capacity day where only light, low-stakes work is realistic — emails, small reviews, reading, no deep integration work — how many of the five days can that 20-hour task actually count on?
contentSections.explanation: Four, not five — and that's the optimistic version, assuming the other four are genuinely full-capacity days, which they often aren't either. Planning a 20-hour task across five nominal days, at 4 hours a day, silently assumes every single day arrives at full capacity. Losing even one day to a crash isn't a minor slip against that plan — it's a 20% capacity loss with zero slack built in to absorb it, because the plan never budgeted for the day existing.

contentSections.body:
The fix isn't estimating fewer hours — the task still takes what it takes. It's scoping the *delivery* around capacity that varies, instead of around a five-day week that assumes it doesn't. Two moves do most of the work:

**Build the deliverable in checkable stages**, the way a lab in this course is staged — each stage independently useful, each one a real stopping point. A task scoped as five two-hour stages survives a bad day between stage two and stage three. A task scoped as one twenty-hour block doesn't survive a bad day anywhere in the middle; it just stalls.

**Quote a date range or a stage-based delivery, not a single date that assumes five good days in a row.** “Stage 3 of 5 done by Thursday, full delivery by early next week, and I'll flag immediately if a stage slips” is a commitment a variable-capacity week can actually keep. “Done Friday” is a bet against a specific outcome nobody controls.
Stage the deliverable so a bad day stalls one stage, not the whole commitment — and quote delivery in a shape that survives one.

contentSections.title: Building the plan

contentSections.body: Turning “20 hours, staged, variable week” into an actual plan someone can hand a client is the practical part. Here's what goes in it.

contentSections.intro: You're scoping a 20-hour task — rebuild a reporting export with a new data source — for a client who needs it “soon” and doesn't yet know your capacity varies. Assemble the plan you'd actually send them.

fields.prompt: How should the 20 hours be broken into stages?
options: One block: 20 hours, delivered all at once at the end
4–5 stages of roughly 4–5 hours each, each producing something checkable on its own
20 stages of exactly 1 hour each, for maximum granularity
fields.correctValue: 4–5 stages of roughly 4–5 hours each, each producing something checkable on its own
fields.feedback: Matches how labs in this track are staged, for the same reason: fine enough that one bad day loses a stage, not the project, coarse enough that each stage is still a meaningful unit of finished work rather than busywork to report progress.

fields.prompt: How should capacity variability show up in the date you quote?
options: Don't mention it — quote the fastest realistic date and hope for good days
Quote a date range built from a realistic mix of day types, and say so
Refuse to give any date until the work is finished
fields.correctValue: Quote a date range built from a realistic mix of day types, and say so
fields.feedback: A range grounded in a stated assumption (“assuming one lighter day this week, which is typical”) is a real commitment the client can plan around. A single best-case date is a promise you're not actually in control of keeping.

fields.prompt: What do you tell the client about how you work, if anything?
options: Nothing — it's not their business how you manage your time
A brief, factual note that your schedule includes planned lower-capacity days, without over-explaining or apologizing
A detailed medical explanation to justify the timeline
fields.correctValue: A brief, factual note that your schedule includes planned lower-capacity days, without over-explaining or apologizing
fields.feedback: This mirrors the reviewer-profile instinct from earlier in the track: state the constraint as a fact about how the work is delivered, not as an apology. “My schedule includes planned lighter days, which is reflected in the range above” tells the client what they need — how to plan — without asking them to manage your health for you.

fields.prompt: What happens if a stage slips?
options: Say nothing until the final delivery date and hope to make it up
Flag it as soon as it's known, with the specific stage affected and the revised date
Silently extend every remaining stage by the same amount without telling anyone
fields.correctValue: Flag it as soon as it's known, with the specific stage affected and the revised date
fields.feedback: This is what staged delivery is actually for — it turns “the whole thing is late, sorry” (discovered at the deadline) into “stage 3 is a day behind, here's the new date for stage 4” (known days earlier, while there's still time to do something about it).

contentSections.synthesis: A plan built this way isn't hedged, it's accurate: staged so a bad day costs a stage, dated as a range with a stated reason, disclosed as fact rather than apology, and updated the moment a stage slips rather than at the deadline. That's a plan a variable-capacity week can actually deliver on — which is the only kind worth quoting.

contentSections.body: Staged, ranged, disclosed as fact, updated the moment a stage slips — that's what makes a scope survive contact with a real week.

title: Renegotiating When the Estimate Was Wrong
description: What to do — and say — the moment it's clear an estimate is going to miss, before the deadline arrives and the conversation gets harder.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize the earliest reliable signal that an estimate is going to miss
Renegotiate a blown estimate in a way that preserves trust

contentSections.title: The signal arrives before the deadline does

contentSections.body: The estimate was 70 minutes. Forty minutes in, correctness review has already turned up a second bug the pattern-match didn't predict, and the “known edge cases” list just grew by two. Nothing about the deadline has changed yet. Something about the estimate already has.

contentSections.scenario: Across a dozen renegotiated estimates a developer has run in the past, the ones that went badly — tense conversation, damaged trust, client surprised — share something in common with each other that the ones that went well don't.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely difference between the renegotiations that went well and the ones that went badly?

options.label: The badly-handled ones were bigger misses in absolute hours
The badly-handled ones were raised close to or after the original deadline; the well-handled ones were raised as soon as the signal appeared
The badly-handled ones involved clients who were generally harder to work with

feedback.size: Size matters less than it seems like it should — a small miss disclosed late still reads as “you knew and didn't say,” and a large miss disclosed early still reads as “thanks for telling me now, while we can still do something.” Timing, not magnitude, is what a client actually reacts to.
feedback.timing: This is the pattern. A renegotiation raised the moment the signal appears — while there's still time to change scope, add resources, or adjust the deadline — reads as competent risk management. The identical renegotiation raised at or after the deadline reads as either incompetence or concealment, because by then the client has already made downstream decisions based on a date that quietly stopped being true.
feedback.client: Some clients genuinely are harder to work with, but that's not the pattern that predicts a bad renegotiation — the same client reacts very differently to the same-sized miss depending entirely on how early they hear about it.

contentSections.mechanism: **The cost of a blown estimate is mostly a function of when it's disclosed, not how large it is.** Every day between “you know it's going to miss” and “you say so” is a day the client is making decisions on a number that's already wrong without knowing it — scheduling a launch, promising a stakeholder, turning down other work. Disclosing the moment the signal is real, not the moment it's certain, is what keeps the miss a scheduling problem instead of a trust problem.

contentSections.body: The cost of a blown estimate comes from when you disclose it, not from how big the miss is. Raise it at the first real signal, not the deadline.

contentSections.title: Renegotiating without relitigating the original number

contentSections.body: There's a version of this conversation that turns into defending the original estimate, and a version that turns into fixing the plan. Only one of them is useful to the person on the other end of it.

contentSections.title: The estimate that's already wrong at the 40-minute mark
contentSections.opening: You quoted 70 minutes for a ticket. At 40 minutes in, you've hit a second unpredicted bug and the edge-case list has grown. You're now confident the real number is closer to 2.5 hours. The deadline the client is working toward is still four hours away.

decide.situation: You could keep working silently and hope to claw the time back, or say something now.
decide.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Keep working, say nothing unless you actually miss the deadline
choices.consequence: You finish at the 2.5-hour mark, ten minutes past the client's deadline, having said nothing until it was already too late to plan around.

choices.label: Message now: here's what changed, here's the revised estimate, here's what it means for the deadline

response.situation: You send: “Found a second issue the pattern-match didn't predict — [specifics]. Revised estimate is 2.5 hours total, not 70 minutes. That puts me about 40 minutes past your deadline if I keep going as planned. Two options: I can ship a version that handles the two bugs I've found and defer the third edge case to a fast follow-up tomorrow, or take the extra 40 minutes now. Your call.” The client replies: “Why didn't the estimate account for this the first time?”
response.question: How do you answer?

choices.label: Explain in detail why the original estimate was reasonable given what was known then
choices.consequence: You're now defending a number instead of fixing a plan. The client didn't ask for a justification of the past; they asked what happens next, and the conversation stalls on something that can't be changed.

choices.label: Acknowledge it briefly, then point at the two live options and ask which they'd prefer
choices.consequence: You say: “Fair question — it's a real gap in the original scope reading, not something I could see in advance. Which of the two options works better for you?” The client picks the deferred-edge-case option in about ten seconds.

silent_missed.summary: The deadline is missed with no warning, and the client's first information about the problem is the problem itself, already happened.
silent_missed.lesson: This is the version that costs trust regardless of the actual size of the miss. Forty minutes late with zero warning reads as either incompetence or concealment — the same forty minutes, flagged three hours earlier, reads as a professional managing a normal surprise.

defended.summary: The relationship survives, but the conversation burned time and goodwill relitigating a decision that can't be unmade, instead of spending that time on the decision that's still open.
defended.lesson: A client asking “why didn't you see this coming” is very often not actually demanding an audit of your original reasoning — they're expressing surprise while they orient. Answering the audit question at length, instead of briefly acknowledging it and moving to the choice that's still available, spends the conversation on the part that can't change.

resolved.summary: The client makes an informed choice within the same message thread, the deadline conversation is closed within minutes, and the relevant piece of new information — what actually went wrong — was disclosed rather than buried.
resolved.lesson: Briefly owning the gap and immediately offering the live options does two things a long defense doesn't: it respects that the client's real question is “what happens now,” and it demonstrates — by example, not by claim — that surprises get surfaced fast around here, which is the reputation that makes the next renegotiation go easily too.

contentSections.body: When a client asks why the estimate missed, a brief acknowledgment and the live options beats a defense of a number that can't be changed anymore.

title: Practice — Estimate Seven Briefs and State What Would Break Each One
description: Seven drills across estimating, unknowns and renegotiation. No new concepts — this is where separating generation time from review time stops being something you read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the estimating procedure to unfamiliar briefs at speed
Name the specific unknown or risk that would break a given estimate

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven briefs, each needing an estimate and a named risk. Ordered from where the lessons left off to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing here expires.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Estimate a Real Brief and Track the Variance
description: Estimate a real piece of work using the review-first procedure, do the work, then account honestly for where the estimate and the actual diverged.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a review-first estimate for a real piece of work
Account for variance between an estimate and an actual in specific, checkable terms

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every estimate in this module so far has been a worked example on someone else's brief. This one is yours — a real task, estimated before you start, tracked while you do it, and accounted for honestly afterward.

contentSections.title: Estimate, deliver, account for the difference
contentSections.brief: Pick one real, bounded piece of AI-assisted work you can actually do — from your own backlog, a small open-source issue, or a scoped practice task if nothing real is available. It should be small enough to finish inside this lab's stages (roughly 1–2 hours of actual work) but real enough that the estimate matters.
contentSections.deliverable: An estimate with named parts, the actual time spent per part, and a written account of where the difference came from — specific enough that someone else could learn your estimating blind spot from reading it.

stages.title: Write the review-first estimate
stages.instructions: Before touching the code, write an estimate broken into generation, correctness review, test-writing and integration — the same four lines from lesson two. For each review and test line, name the specific thing you're checking for or the specific edge case you expect to add, not just a number.
stages.checkpoint: You have four named lines with a minute figure each, and the review/test lines each name something specific.

stages.title: Name the unknowns
stages.instructions: List anything from lesson three's evidence-stack pattern that could change the estimate or the correct behavior — not implementation trivia. For each, state what it would cost if it goes the expensive way.
stages.checkpoint: At least one real unknown is named with its cost, or you've concluded honestly that there isn't one — which is itself worth stating.

stages.title: Do the work and log the actual
stages.instructions: Do the task. Log actual time against each of the four lines as you go, not from memory afterward — memory rounds toward the original estimate. If a stage runs long enough that you'd have renegotiated a real deadline, note the moment you noticed, per lesson five.
stages.checkpoint: You have real, in-the-moment time figures for each line, not a reconstruction.

stages.title: Write the variance account
stages.instructions: For each line where estimate and actual differ by more than 20%, write one or two sentences on what specifically caused the gap — an unknown that turned out to matter, a review cost you underweighted, a test case you didn't predict. “It just took longer” is not an account; name the specific thing.
stages.checkpoint: Every significant variance has a specific, named cause — not a vague acknowledgment that the estimate was off.

rubric.criterion: The original estimate has four named, specific parts
rubric.meets: Generation, correctness review, test-writing and integration each have a minute figure and, for the review/test lines, a named thing being checked — not just a total.

rubric.criterion: At least one real unknown was named in advance
rubric.meets: A specific unknown and its potential cost appear before the work started — or an honest, reasoned statement that none applied.

rubric.criterion: Actual time was logged in the moment, per line
rubric.meets: The actual figures are per-line and clearly not reconstructed from memory after the fact.

rubric.criterion: Every significant variance has a specific cause
rubric.meets: Each gap over roughly 20% is explained by a named, checkable reason — not “it took longer than expected.”

rubric.criterion: The account would teach someone else your actual blind spot
rubric.meets: A reader could point at one sentence and say what this person systematically underestimates.

contentSections.body: An estimate that tracks its own variance, by named part, is the fastest way to find out what you systematically get wrong — and the only way to stop getting it wrong the same way twice.

title: Checkpoint — Estimating and Scoping
description: Ten questions across the module. Ungraded, untimed — the first module of this phase, so every question pulls from here.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Estimating and Scoping
contentSections.framing: This is the first module of the phase, so all ten questions pull from here — there's nothing earlier yet to space against.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: What does AI generation speed actually shorten?

options.label: The whole job, roughly proportionally
Mainly the typing/generation step itself — review and integration are largely unaffected
Nothing measurable

questions.explanation: Generation collapses toward zero. Review time is set by how much trust the result needs, which doesn't change because the typing got faster.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: A team consistently underestimates AI-assisted tickets by a similar margin, ticket after ticket. What does that pattern suggest?

options.label: The estimating formula still charges for typing time that mostly isn't being spent
The team needs more training
The AI tool is unreliable

questions.explanation: A steady, similarly-sized miss across varied tickets points at the model, not the people or the tool — the old typing-time formula is silently omitting the biggest current cost.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: In a review-first estimate, what should the parts be?

options.label: Generation, correctness review, test-writing, integration — named separately
One number covering the whole task
Lines of generated code times a fixed rate

questions.explanation: A total with no named parts is a guess with a decimal point. Named, checkable parts make the estimate defensible and re-checkable.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: Two variables move correctness-review time independently of how much code exists. What are they?

options.label: How familiar you are with the code, and what it costs if you're wrong
How fast you type, and how many tests exist
The programming language, and the time of day

questions.explanation: Unfamiliarity and consequence both push review time up independently of lines of code — a one-line change to unfamiliar payments code can rightly take longer to review than fifty lines of familiar code.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: What makes an unknown worth naming in a scoping conversation, versus just building it and finding out?

options.label: It changes the estimate or the correct behavior of the thing being built
It's anything you're not 100% sure about
It's a technical implementation detail like an exact method name

questions.explanation: The Slack-notification example split unknowns into two piles: things that change scope or correctness (worth naming) and things that are just coding details (not worth flagging).

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: Why is “5–7 business days” with no explanation a bad estimate, even though it's honestly hedged?

options.label: It doesn't name what the two-day range depends on, so the client can't act on the uncertainty
Ranges are always unprofessional
It should have been a single exact number

questions.explanation: A range with no named cause is the same guess with a hedge stapled on. Naming what the range depends on turns it into a decision the client can act on.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: How should a 20-hour task be scoped across a week where capacity varies day to day?

options.label: Staged into 4–5 independently checkable chunks, quoted as a date range
One 20-hour block delivered at the very end
Quoted as a single best-case date assuming five full-capacity days

questions.explanation: Staging means a bad day stalls one stage, not the whole commitment. A single best-case date is a bet against something nobody controls.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: How should a developer disclose that their schedule includes planned lower-capacity days?

options.label: Briefly and factually, without over-explaining or apologizing
Not at all — it's private
With a detailed personal explanation to justify the timeline

questions.explanation: Stated as a fact about how the work is delivered, the same way the reviewer-profile lab earlier in the track framed limitations as method, not apology.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: What determines whether a blown estimate costs trust — the size of the miss, or something else?

options.label: Mostly when it's disclosed, not how big it is
Only the absolute number of hours missed
Whether the client is generally easy to work with

questions.explanation: A renegotiation raised at the first real signal reads as competent risk management; the identical miss raised at the deadline reads as concealment — same size, opposite reaction.

questions.from: This module — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: A client asks, mid-renegotiation, “why didn't the original estimate account for this?” What's the better response?

options.label: A brief acknowledgment, then point at the live options and ask which they'd prefer
A detailed defense of why the original estimate was reasonable
No response — just keep working

questions.explanation: A long defense spends the conversation on a number that can't change anymore. Briefly owning the gap and moving to the still-open decision respects what the client actually needs next.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: You Shipped It, So It's Yours
description: Why authorship of AI-generated code doesn't transfer to the tool, no matter how little of it you typed — and what that means the moment something breaks.

learningObjectives.text: State who is accountable for AI-generated code once it ships
Distinguish authorship from typing

contentSections.title: "I didn't write that" isn't a defense

contentSections.body: A production incident takes down checkout for eleven minutes. In the retro, the developer who merged the change says: "the AI wrote that part, I just reviewed it." The room goes quiet, not because anyone doubts it's true, but because it doesn't change anything about what happens next.

contentSections.scenario: Three developers each ship a bug that reaches production. Developer A typed every line by hand and missed an edge case. Developer B had an AI tool generate the function, reviewed it, and missed the same edge case. Developer C had an AI tool generate the function and merged it without reading it at all.
contentSections.question: Which of these three is accountable for the bug reaching production?

options.label: Only A and C — B reviewed it, so the tool shares responsibility
All three, equally — the code shipped under each of their names either way
Only A — B and C can reasonably point at the tool

feedback.a_and_c: It's tempting to think review dilutes responsibility, but B's review didn't transfer anything to the tool — it just means B had a chance to catch the bug and didn't. That's the same accountability A has, for the same reason: the code shipped under B's name.
feedback.all: Right, and B and C differ from each other in a way that matters even though both are accountable: C skipped the one step that was actually theirs to do. Merging without reading isn't a smaller version of writing bad code by hand — it's closer to negligence, because reviewing what you ship is the part of the job that AI generation didn't remove.
feedback.only_a: Pointing at the tool doesn't work for B or C, and for a specific reason: a tool has no legal or professional standing to be accountable for anything. Accountability has to land somewhere, and "the AI did it" is not an answer any client, employer, or court accepts — it just describes how the code was produced, not who's responsible for it.

contentSections.concept: **Merging a change is an act of authorship, regardless of how the diff was produced.** The moment you hit merge, approve, or ship, you are asserting — to your team, your client, and often contractually — that this code is correct and yours to stand behind. Nothing about how efficiently it was produced changes what that assertion means.

contentSections.body: This isn't a new rule invented for AI tooling. It's the same rule that already applied to a developer who copy-pasted from Stack Overflow, adapted a library example, or had a junior write a function they then approved. The person who merges has always owned the merge. What's new is the volume — a tool that can generate a whole feature in ninety seconds makes it much easier to merge something you haven't actually understood, because the friction that used to force understanding (the time it took to type it) is gone.
Merging is authorship. "The AI wrote it" describes production, not accountability — and accountability doesn't have anywhere else to go.

contentSections.title: What "yours" actually obligates you to

contentSections.body: Owning a change doesn't mean you have to have typed it, or even to be able to reproduce it from memory. It means something more specific and more checkable than that.

contentSections.scenario: A developer is deciding what "I own this code" should actually require of them before merging an AI-generated change.
contentSections.question: Which of these are things ownership genuinely requires?

items.label: Being able to explain, to another engineer, why the code works and what it would do in a case not shown in the diff
Having actually considered what happens if this specific change is wrong
Having typed every character of the final code by hand
Being able to reproduce the exact code from memory a week later

explanation.explain: This is the real bar: if you can't explain what a piece of code does in a case the diff didn't show, you don't actually understand it well enough to have reviewed it — you've read it, which is different.
explanation.risk: Ownership means having asked "what does this break if it's wrong" and acted accordingly — more scrutiny for a payments function than for a tooltip's copy.
explanation.typed: Typing was never actually the requirement, even before AI tools existed — it's just that typing used to be hard to skip, so it correlated with understanding. It was never the thing itself.
explanation.memorize: Nobody, with or without AI tools, is expected to memorize code verbatim. Understanding what it does and why is the requirement; recall is not.

contentSections.synthesis: **Ownership is being able to explain and defend the code, and having genuinely weighed what happens if it's wrong — not having typed it or being able to recite it.** That's a real, checkable bar, and it's exactly the bar the rest of this module builds on: it's what makes disclosure honest instead of performative, and what determines when refusing to review something is the right call.

contentSections.body: Ownership means you can explain the code and you've weighed what happens if it's wrong — not that you typed it or can recite it.

title: What Generated Code May Carry With It
description: License provenance, training-data risk, and how to check what an AI-generated snippet might be bringing with it before it ships.

learningObjectives.text: Identify signals that generated code may carry license or provenance risk
Apply a check before shipping code that resembles a known, licensed source

contentSections.title: Code doesn't arrive from nowhere

contentSections.body: A generated utility function looks completely unremarkable — sort a list of objects by three fields with tie-breaking. Then someone recognizes it, verbatim, comment and all, from a specific open-source library with a copyleft license nobody on the project agreed to.

contentSections.problem: An AI tool generates a 40-line function for parsing a specific, unusual binary file format, including a distinctive comment: "// handles the legacy v2 header quirk, see spec appendix C." You don't recognize the codebase this came from, but the specificity feels off for something generated fresh. What do you check before merging?

steps.label: Notice the specificity signal
steps.work: A comment referencing a specific, named external spec ("appendix C") in a codebase that has never mentioned that spec is a strong sign this is reproduced from somewhere, not generated fresh from a general pattern.
steps.why: Generated boilerplate for common patterns (a REST handler, a form validator) is low-risk precisely because there's no single source it's plausibly copied from — thousands of near-identical examples exist. A distinctive comment about a specific, obscure spec section is the opposite: it suggests one identifiable origin.

steps.label: Search for the distinctive string
steps.work: Search a code search engine or the web for the exact comment text or a distinctive variable name from the snippet.
steps.why: This is the cheapest possible check — thirty seconds — and it directly answers the question "does this exist, verbatim, somewhere with a license attached?"

steps.label: If a match is found, check its license
steps.work: Suppose the search finds this exact function, comment included, in a GitHub repo under GPL-3.0. That license requires derivative works to also be GPL-licensed — likely incompatible with a proprietary commercial codebase.
steps.why: This is the actual risk: not that the code is bad, but that shipping it may obligate the project to license terms nobody agreed to, or may constitute a license violation the moment it's caught.

steps.label: Decide, don't guess
steps.work: Either rewrite the function from the spec directly (not from the flagged snippet), or get explicit sign-off from whoever handles licensing at the company, providing the source found.
steps.why: This is not a decision to make alone by feel — company policy on license risk varies, and it's a legal question, not an engineering one, once a real match is found. The engineer's job is to surface it clearly, not to privately decide it's probably fine.

faded.problem: A second case: an AI tool generates a well-known sorting algorithm implementation with generic variable names (a, b, temp) and no comments referencing anything specific. It closely resembles the textbook version of the algorithm that appears in hundreds of tutorials and codebases.

blanks.prompt: Is the specificity signal from step one present here — distinctive, or generic-and-common?
blanks.answer: generic and common
blanks.why: A textbook algorithm implementation with generic names doesn't point at one identifiable source — it's closer to a fact of computer science than a specific author's expression, which is part of why algorithms like this are rarely the subject of license disputes.

blanks.prompt: Should you still spend 30 seconds searching for it, given step two's reasoning?
blanks.answer: not necessary, low value here
blanks.why: The 30-second check is cheap, but it's not free of judgment about when to spend it — a distinctive, spec-referencing comment justifies it; a generic sort implementation that resembles a thousand tutorials doesn't carry the same signal, so the check has low expected value here.

blanks.prompt: What's the general rule for when the license-risk check is worth running? (one sentence)
blanks.answer: run it when the code is unusually specific, distinctive, or resembles a named/identifiable source, not for generic common patterns
accept: when it looks copied from somewhere specific
distinctive or unusual code, not generic boilerplate
blanks.why: The rule scales the check to the signal: distinctive, spec-referencing, unusually specific code gets the search; common, generic patterns that exist in thousands of interchangeable forms don't need it every time.

contentSections.procedure: **Distinctive, specific, or spec-referencing code gets a quick provenance check before it ships. Generic, common patterns usually don't need one.** The check itself is cheap — search for a distinctive string — and the decision on a real match is not the individual engineer's to make alone; it goes to whoever owns licensing, with the evidence attached.

contentSections.body: Distinctive or spec-referencing generated code gets a cheap provenance check before merge. A real match goes to whoever owns licensing — it's not an engineering call to make alone.

contentSections.title: The risk that isn't a license

contentSections.body: License is the checkable risk. There's a second one that's fuzzier and just as real: code that's subtly wrong in a way that reflects an outdated or insecure pattern the tool learned from somewhere, with nothing to search for at all.

contentSections.question: This code has no distinctive comment, no identifiable source to search for, and runs without error. What's the actual risk here, and what kind of risk is it?

options.label: A license risk — this pattern likely came from a specific copyrighted tutorial
A currency risk — MD5 is a known-broken hashing algorithm for passwords, and the tool generated a pattern that was once common but is now considered unsafe
No real risk — the function runs correctly and returns a hash

feedback.license: There's no distinctive marker here to search for — this is generic-looking code, which is exactly what makes it a different kind of risk than the license example. Nothing about it points at a specific copyrighted source.
feedback.currency: Correct, and this is the risk lesson three of this module and the wider track return to: MD5 is fast and reversible-by-brute-force by modern standards, and using it for password storage is a known, serious security mistake — but the code runs without error and looks plausible, because it was a common pattern in older, now-outdated material the tool may have learned from. There's no distinctive string to search for and no license to check. The only defense is knowing enough about the domain to recognize an outdated pattern regardless of how confidently it's presented.
feedback.none: It runs and returns a hash, which is exactly why this risk is dangerous — nothing about it fails loudly. The function "works" in the sense that it executes; it fails in the sense that it stores passwords in a way attackers can crack quickly, which won't show up in a test suite or a code review that only checks whether the function behaves as intended.

contentSections.flawExplanation: License risk is checkable by searching for a distinctive string. This second kind of risk — a plausible-looking pattern that's outdated, insecure, or was common practice years ago and no longer is — has no string to search for and no error to catch it. It's caught only by domain knowledge: knowing that password hashing needs a slow, salted algorithm (like bcrypt or argon2), not a fast general-purpose hash like MD5 or SHA-256 used directly. This is a specific instance of a general fact about generated code: fluency in generating plausible code is not the same as correctness, and the gap is widest exactly in domains — cryptography, security, concurrency — where "looks right" and "is right" diverge the most.

contentSections.body: License risk is searchable. Outdated-or-insecure-pattern risk isn't — it's caught only by knowing the domain well enough to recognize plausible-but-wrong.

title: Client Policies, NDAs, and What You May Paste Into a Tool
description: What actually leaves your machine when you use an AI coding tool, and why a client's NDA can make that a real problem regardless of what the tool's own privacy policy says.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a given piece of client code or data is safe to paste into an AI tool
Identify the specific clause types in client agreements that govern this

contentSections.title: Pasting is disclosure

contentSections.body: A contractor, stuck on a bug, pastes forty lines of the client's production code — including a hardcoded internal API endpoint and a comment referencing an unreleased product — into a public AI chat tool to ask for help. The tool's answer is genuinely useful. The client's NDA, which the contractor signed and didn't reread, says client code may not be disclosed to any third party without written consent.

contentSections.scenario: Two contractors both use AI coding tools daily on client work. One has never had an issue. The other gets a pointed question from a client's security team about where their code has been pasted, after noticing unusual API usage patterns.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely difference in how the two contractors are actually using these tools, given that both use them constantly?

options.label: One uses a faster tool than the other

One treats a company-approved, contractually-covered AI tool as the default and is deliberate about what leaves the machine; the other pastes freely into whatever tool is open, without checking what the client agreement actually says
One is simply more careful by personality

feedback.speed: Tool speed has nothing to do with what data leaves the machine or under what terms — this isn't a performance question.
feedback.policy: This is the real mechanism. "Using an AI tool" isn't one thing — it's a decision, made or not made deliberately, about which tool, under what data-handling terms, for which category of code. A contractor operating inside an approved tool with an enterprise agreement covering data retention and training-use is in a completely different position than one pasting into whatever's open in a browser tab, even though from the outside both just look like "using AI to code faster."
feedback.personality: Personality-based carefulness isn't a reliable system — it depends on remembering to be careful every single time, under deadline pressure, which is exactly when people paste first and think later. A policy — a default tool, a rule about what categories of code never get pasted anywhere — doesn't depend on remembering.

contentSections.mechanism: **The risk isn't the tool; it's the absence of a rule about what goes into it.** An NDA typically restricts disclosure to third parties — and a general-purpose AI tool, unless specifically covered by an enterprise agreement with the client's own data-handling terms, is a third party. The fix is deciding in advance, per client, what's covered and what isn't — not deciding it fresh, under deadline pressure, every time something's stuck.

contentSections.body: An AI tool not specifically covered by the client's agreement is a third party. Decide what's safe to paste in advance, per client — not under deadline pressure.

contentSections.title: What actually needs checking, and where

contentSections.body: Reading an entire NDA before every prompt isn't realistic. A short, specific set of things to check once, per client, is.

contentSections.scenario: Before using a general-purpose AI coding tool on a new client engagement, a contractor is deciding what to check and what's realistic to check once versus every time.
contentSections.question: Which of these are worth checking once at the start of an engagement, before any code gets pasted anywhere?

items.label: Whether the contract's confidentiality clause defines "third party" broadly enough to include AI tools, or has specific language about AI tool use
Whether the client operates under a data-residency requirement (common in healthcare, finance, government contracts) that a general-purpose tool's data handling might violate
Whether the client already has an approved, covered AI tool that should be the default instead of a personal one
What font the client's coding style guide specifies
What the AI tool's own data-retention and training-use policy actually says, not what's assumed about it

explanation.confidentiality_clause: This is the specific clause that determines whether pasting code into a tool is a breach at all. Some contracts explicitly permit AI tool use with conditions; some are silent (which is its own risk); some prohibit it outright.
explanation.data_residency: A requirement that data never leave a specific jurisdiction is a hard constraint that many general-purpose AI tools, with servers and processing wherever their infrastructure happens to be, may simply violate regardless of intent.
explanation.approved_tools: If the client already pays for and covers a specific tool under their own agreement, that's the default — not a personal subscription to something else with different terms.
explanation.font: Not a confidentiality or data-handling question at all — this belongs in the technical style guide, not the pre-engagement risk check.
explanation.retention: Assuming a tool doesn't retain or train on inputs, without checking, is exactly the kind of unverified belief that turns into the security team's pointed question later. The actual policy, read once, is what the confidentiality clause needs to be checked against.

contentSections.synthesis: **Four things, checked once at the start of an engagement — the confidentiality clause's third-party language, any data-residency requirement, whether an approved tool already exists, and the actual (not assumed) retention policy of the tool in question — cover almost every real case.** That's a fifteen-minute check at the start of a contract, not a daily burden, and it's what turns "I use AI tools, is that a problem?" from a live risk into a settled question.

contentSections.body: Four checks, once per engagement: the confidentiality clause's third-party language, data-residency requirements, whether an approved tool exists, and the tool's actual retention policy.

title: Disclosure That Is Honest Without Being Theatre
description: Writing an AI-use disclosure that tells a client something true and useful, instead of either hiding the tool or performing a caveat nobody needed.

learningObjectives.text: Write a disclosure statement that conveys real, actionable information
Distinguish useful disclosure from disclosure theatre

contentSections.title: Two ways to get disclosure wrong

contentSections.body: One developer's PR description says nothing about how the code was produced. Another's says, on every single PR regardless of content: "Note: parts of this code were AI-assisted and should be reviewed with appropriate caution." Neither one tells the reviewer anything they can actually use.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer is deciding how much scrutiny to give three PRs. PR 1's description: nothing about how it was produced. PR 2's description: the boilerplate caution note, unchanged from every other PR this developer has ever submitted. PR 3's description: "Generated the CRUD scaffolding and tests with AI, matches existing patterns exactly, low-risk. The retry-logic in the payment-webhook handler (lines 40–65) I wrote and reasoned through manually — that's the part I'd focus review time on, since it changes how we handle partial failures."
contentSections.question: Which disclosure actually changes how the reviewer should spend their time?

options.label: PR 2 — at least it mentions AI was involved
PR 3 — it says specifically what to trust more and what to focus review on
None of them — a reviewer should review everything equally regardless of disclosure

feedback.pr2: PR 2's note is true on every PR this developer submits, which means it's informationally empty — a reviewer reading it learns nothing they didn't already assume, and nothing about where to actually look harder. It's the disclosure equivalent of a boilerplate legal disclaimer: technically accurate, functionally useless.
feedback.pr3: Right. PR 3 does the actual job of disclosure: it tells the reviewer where confidence is already high (pattern-matched scaffolding) and where it's genuinely lower and reasoning was novel (the retry logic), which is exactly where review time is worth spending. That's a disclosure a reviewer can act on.
feedback.none: In principle a thorough reviewer reviews everything hard regardless — but reviewers, like everyone, have finite time and attention, and real review effort gets allocated unevenly whether anyone admits it or not. A disclosure that honestly says where the risk actually concentrates makes that allocation better instead of pretending it doesn't happen.

contentSections.concept: **Useful disclosure is specific to the change: what was generated versus reasoned through by hand, and where the author's own confidence is lower.** A disclosure that's identical across every PR, regardless of content, isn't disclosure — it's a habit that happens to use the word "AI." The test is whether removing the sentence would lose the reviewer any actual information.

contentSections.body: This same test applies outside code review. A client-facing AI-use policy that says "we may use AI tools in our work" and stops there is legally covering the writer, maybe, but it's not informing the client of anything they could act on. A policy that says which categories of work get AI assistance, what review step every AI-assisted change goes through before it ships, and what happens if something generated turns out to be wrong, is one the client can actually evaluate — and, if they want, push back on.
The test for real disclosure: would removing this sentence cost the reader actual information? If not, it's theatre wearing the shape of honesty.

contentSections.title: Writing it for a specific reader

contentSections.body: The same underlying facts about how you work need to sound different depending on who's reading — not because the facts change, but because what the reader needs to do with them does.

contentSections.intro: You use AI tools for roughly 60% of your generated code, always with a manual review pass, and you're more cautious on anything touching auth, payments, or data migrations, where you write the core logic by hand and use AI only for boilerplate and tests. Build a one-paragraph disclosure appropriate to each reader.

fields.prompt: What should a client-facing disclosure (e.g. in a proposal or SOW) emphasize?
options: A generic mention that AI tools may be used
What's covered by AI assistance, what review step every change goes through, and where extra caution applies (auth, payments, migrations)
A technical list of which specific AI models and tools are used
fields.correctValue: What's covered by AI assistance, what review step every change goes through, and where extra caution applies (auth, payments, migrations)
fields.feedback: A client cares about process and risk allocation, not brand names. "Extra caution on auth, payments, and migrations, always reviewed before merge" tells them exactly what they're paying for and where the higher-risk areas get more of your own direct attention.

fields.prompt: What should a per-PR disclosure emphasize, per lesson four's PR 3 example?
options: A boilerplate caution note identical across every PR
Nothing — code review shouldn't need to know this
Which specific parts of this PR were generated versus hand-reasoned, and where review attention should concentrate
fields.correctValue: Which specific parts of this PR were generated versus hand-reasoned, and where review attention should concentrate
fields.feedback: This is the change-specific version of the same principle — useful because it's different every time, tied to what's actually in this diff, not a fixed sentence.

fields.prompt: If something AI-assisted ships broken and causes an incident, what belongs in the postmortem's disclosure?
options: Omit how the code was produced — it's not relevant to the fix
State plainly that the code was AI-generated and reviewed, and name specifically what the review step missed and why
Emphasize that the AI tool is at fault
fields.correctValue: State plainly that the code was AI-generated and reviewed, and name specifically what the review step missed and why
fields.feedback: This connects straight back to lesson one: the tool isn't accountable, the reviewer is — so the honest postmortem statement names the actual gap in the review process (a missed edge case, a check that didn't happen) rather than either hiding the tool's involvement or using it as a shield.

contentSections.synthesis: The underlying practice doesn't change across these three contexts — what changes is which part of it the specific reader needs in order to act. A client needs process and risk allocation. A reviewer needs today's specific confidence map. A postmortem needs the specific gap that let something through. Writing all three as the same generic sentence would satisfy none of the readers; writing them specifically to each is the actual work of honest disclosure.

contentSections.body: The same practice needs a different disclosure for a client, a reviewer, and a postmortem — because each reader needs to act on something different.

title: When to Refuse Work You Can't Review
description: Recognizing the point where a piece of generated code is beyond what you can genuinely verify, and what to do about it instead of shipping it anyway.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a change exceeds your ability to genuinely review it
Choose an appropriate response when asked to ship code you can't verify

contentSections.title: Fluent isn't the same as understood

contentSections.body: An AI tool generates a 200-line concurrency fix for a race condition in a distributed job queue — a domain the developer reviewing it has never worked in professionally. It reads fluently. Every line looks reasonable. None of that means the developer can tell you whether it actually fixes the race condition or introduces a subtler one.

contentSections.scenario: A developer merges a generated concurrency fix that reads cleanly and passes all existing tests. Three weeks later, a new, harder-to-reproduce race condition appears in production, introduced by the "fix." In the retro, the developer says: "it looked right, and it passed review."
contentSections.question: What actually went wrong here, most precisely?

options.label: The AI tool made an error, which is an acceptable and unavoidable risk of using it
The developer reviewed something outside what they could genuinely verify, and treated "reads cleanly and passes existing tests" as equivalent to "is correct"
The existing test suite was inadequate, which is the real root cause

feedback.tool_error: The tool producing an imperfect first draft isn't the failure — that's expected and normal, which is why review exists. The failure is specifically that the review step, the one safeguard that's supposed to catch exactly this, didn't actually verify what it needed to.
feedback.review_gap: This is the real mechanism, and it's the same one from lesson one's ownership standard: "reads cleanly" and "passes the tests that already existed" are both weak signals for concurrency-correctness specifically, because race conditions are precisely the class of bug that reads fine and often doesn't show up in a normal test run — you need reasoning about interleavings, not code that looks tidy.
feedback.tests: The test suite not catching a subtle race condition is common and not unique to this case — race conditions are notoriously hard to catch with ordinary tests, which is exactly why generated concurrency code specifically needs a different kind of review than "does it read okay and pass what's there," not just better tests after the fact.

contentSections.mechanism: **Code can be fluent, pass existing tests, and still be outside what a given reviewer can actually verify — and fluency is a particularly bad signal for concurrency, security, and other domains where correctness depends on reasoning the reader can't do just by reading.** The gap between "I read it and it seems fine" and "I actually verified this is correct" is exactly where fluent-but-wrong code gets through, and it's widest in domains that require specialized reasoning the reviewer doesn't have.

contentSections.body: Fluent and tested are weak signals in domains — concurrency, cryptography, security — where correctness needs reasoning the reader can't do just by reading.

contentSections.title: What to actually do about it

contentSections.body: Recognizing you're out of your depth is the easy half. Saying so, to a manager or a client waiting on the ticket, is the half that costs something — and it's the one this lesson is actually about.

contentSections.title: The concurrency fix you can't actually verify
contentSections.opening: You're the only developer available on a small team. A generated fix for a production race condition looks plausible, passes CI, and needs to ship today per the incident timeline. You don't have deep concurrency expertise and can't honestly say you've verified it's correct, just that it looks reasonable.

decide.situation: The incident channel is waiting on an update.
decide.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Ship it — it passes CI and looks right, and something is better than nothing during an active incident
choices.consequence: It ships. Whether it's actually correct is now unknown to everyone, including you, and nobody downstream knows that.

choices.label: Sit on it and say nothing while you try to teach yourself enough concurrency theory to be sure
choices.consequence: Hours pass. The incident continues. Eventually someone asks what's taking so long, and you explain for the first time that you're not confident in the fix — information that would have been far more useful an hour ago.

choices.label: Say plainly, now: "this is outside what I can verify — it looks plausible but I can't confirm it's correct, we need someone with concurrency experience or to accept the risk explicitly"

response.situation: The team lead replies: "we don't have anyone else free right now. What are the options?"
response.question: What do you propose?

choices.label: Ship it as a temporary mitigation with explicit, logged acknowledgment that it's unverified, plus a fast-follow to get real review, and extra monitoring on the affected path
Insist on waiting for an expert no matter how long it takes, even though the incident is ongoing and costing the business money every minute

shipped_blind.summary: Nobody with authority to accept the risk knew there was one. If it's wrong, the next incident starts from a worse position: a fix nobody flagged as uncertain.
shipped_blind.lesson: Shipping unverified code silently doesn't just risk being wrong — it risks being wrong invisibly, with no one positioned to have made a different call. The failure isn't shipping under uncertainty during an incident, which is sometimes genuinely necessary; it's shipping under uncertainty that nobody but you knew existed.

silent_delay.summary: The eventual disclosure was honest, but withheld exactly when it was most useful — while there was still time to get help or make an informed call about the risk.
silent_delay.lesson: This mirrors the estimating module's timing lesson exactly: the same true information is far more valuable disclosed early than disclosed late, and trying to privately solve an out-of-depth problem before admitting it exists is often just a slower, quieter version of the same delay.

resolved.summary: The fix ships with the risk explicitly owned by someone with the authority to accept it, monitoring in place, and a real review scheduled — instead of an unverified fix silently standing in for a verified one.
resolved.lesson: Refusing to review something you can't verify doesn't mean refusing to ship anything — it means refusing to let "I looked at it and it seemed fine" quietly stand in for "this was actually verified." Naming the gap explicitly lets someone with the authority to accept the risk actually decide to, instead of the decision happening by default because nobody said anything.

stalled.summary: The incident drags on with no fix deployed while a fully qualified reviewer is tracked down, and the business cost of the outage keeps accumulating the whole time.
