stalled.lesson: Insisting on a perfect reviewer regardless of cost isn't the same virtue as refusing to falsely certify something as verified — the honest move names the real uncertainty and offers a mitigated path forward (monitoring, a fast-follow review, an explicit risk acceptance), rather than treating "wait for the ideal reviewer" as the only acceptable alternative to shipping blind.

contentSections.body: Refusing to falsely certify something as verified isn't refusing to help. Name the gap, let someone with authority decide, and add monitoring — don't let silence make the decision by default.

title: Practice — Decide the Disclosure Obligation in Seven Situations
description: Seven drills across ownership, licensing risk, client agreements and disclosure. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's accountability and disclosure standards to unfamiliar situations
Evaluate what a specific situation actually obligates, versus what it doesn't

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven situations, each needing a decision about ownership, risk, or disclosure. Do them in one sitting or three.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint.

title: Lab — Write Your Own AI-Use Policy for Client Work
description: Produce the one-page policy you'd actually send a client before starting AI-assisted work, covering ownership, licensing risk, confidentiality, and disclosure.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a client-facing AI-use policy grounded in real practice
State disclosure and risk obligations specifically enough to be checkable

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: A client asks, reasonably: "do you use AI tools, and what does that mean for us?" This lab produces the document you'd actually send back — the honest, specific, one-page version, not a boilerplate disclaimer.

contentSections.title: Your AI-use policy
contentSections.brief: Write the one-page AI-use policy you would send a new client before starting work, covering how you use AI tools, what you're accountable for, what gets extra scrutiny, and what you'd do if something goes wrong.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-page AI-use policy a client could read in two minutes and know exactly what they're getting, what's covered, and what happens if something breaks.

stages.title: State the ownership position
stages.instructions: Write one or two sentences stating plainly that you own everything you ship, regardless of how it was produced — the lesson one standard. This is the foundation the rest of the policy sits on.
stages.checkpoint: The ownership statement is unambiguous and doesn't hedge.

stages.title: Name what gets extra scrutiny
stages.instructions: List the categories of work (per your own practice — auth, payments, migrations, or whatever applies) that get more manual review and less AI-generated code, and briefly why. Be specific, not "sensitive areas."
stages.checkpoint: At least two concrete categories are named with a reason each.

stages.title: Write the licensing and confidentiality section
stages.instructions: State what tool(s) you use, what you check before shipping distinctive or unusual generated code (lesson two), and what you will and won't paste into a general-purpose tool given typical NDA terms (lesson three).
stages.checkpoint: A reader would know specifically what's safe and what isn't, not just that you're "careful."

stages.title: Write the disclosure and incident section
stages.instructions: State how you'll disclose AI involvement in a PR or deliverable (lesson four's specific-not-generic standard), and what happens if something AI-assisted ships broken — who's told, how fast, what the postmortem covers.
stages.checkpoint: The disclosure described would pass the lesson-four test: removing it would cost the reader real information.

stages.title: Cut to one page and self-check
stages.instructions: Cut to one page. Read it as the client: would you know what you're getting? Is any sentence a boilerplate disclaimer rather than real information?
stages.checkpoint: Every sentence survives the "would removing this cost the reader information" test.

rubric.criterion: Ownership is stated plainly, with no hedge
rubric.meets: A reader has no doubt who is accountable for shipped code, regardless of how it was produced.

rubric.criterion: Extra-scrutiny categories are specific
rubric.meets: Named categories (not "sensitive code") each have a stated reason, matching real practice from lessons one and two.

rubric.criterion: The licensing/confidentiality section is checkable
rubric.meets: States a specific check and a specific rule about what gets pasted where, not a general assurance of carefulness.

rubric.criterion: The disclosure section passes the theatre test
rubric.meets: Every sentence in it would cost the reader real information if removed — no boilerplate caution note.

rubric.criterion: The incident section names a real process
rubric.meets: States who is told, how fast, and what the postmortem covers if something AI-assisted breaks.

rubric.criterion: It fits on one page and reads as professional
rubric.meets: A client can read it in two minutes and know exactly what they're getting.

contentSections.body: A policy this specific is worth more to a client than a longer one — because every sentence in it is something they could actually hold you to, and something they can actually evaluate before they say yes.

title: Checkpoint — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
description: Ten questions across the module. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
contentSections.framing: This is the second module of the phase, and its own earlier lessons carry all ten questions this time.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Who is accountable when AI-generated code ships a bug, if the developer reviewed it and missed the same issue a hand-written version would have had?

options.label: The developer who merged it — reviewing doesn't transfer responsibility to the tool
The AI tool, since it produced the code
Nobody specifically — it's a shared, diffuse responsibility

questions.explanation: Merging is an act of authorship regardless of how the diff was produced. A tool has no standing to be accountable; the person who shipped it does.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What does "owning" a piece of code actually require, per this module?

options.label: Having typed every character by hand
Being able to explain what it does in cases the diff didn't show, and having weighed what happens if it's wrong
Being able to reproduce it exactly from memory

questions.explanation: Typing and memorization were never the real requirement. Explaining the code's behavior beyond the shown cases, and having considered the risk if it's wrong, is the actual, checkable bar.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What kind of generated code is worth a quick provenance/license search before merging?

options.label: Distinctive, unusually specific, or spec-referencing code
Any code over 10 lines
Only code that fails to compile on the first try

questions.explanation: Generic, common patterns exist in thousands of interchangeable forms and carry low license risk. Distinctive or spec-referencing code points at one identifiable source, which is worth a cheap search.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Why is an outdated-but-plausible pattern (like MD5 for password hashing) a different kind of risk than a license match?

options.label: It's more expensive to fix
There's no distinctive string to search for and no error to catch it — only domain knowledge catches it
It only affects open-source projects

questions.explanation: License risk is searchable. An outdated-or-insecure-but-plausible pattern runs without error and looks fine on a skim — it's caught only by knowing the domain well enough to recognize it.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Why can pasting client code into a general-purpose AI tool be a real NDA problem, even if the tool's own policy sounds reasonable?

options.label: A tool not specifically covered by the client's agreement is a third party, and NDAs typically restrict disclosure to third parties
AI tools are always insecure by default
It's only a problem if the tool is free to use

questions.explanation: The risk isn't the tool's trustworthiness in the abstract — it's whether the specific client agreement's confidentiality clause covers this use, which is a question to check once per engagement, not assume.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Four things worth checking once at the start of a client engagement include the confidentiality clause's third-party language and the AI tool's actual retention policy. What are the other two?

options.label: Any data-residency requirement, and whether an approved tool already exists for this client
The client's preferred code editor, and their git branching strategy
The tool's monthly subscription price, and its uptime guarantee

questions.explanation: Data-residency requirements and an existing approved tool are both hard constraints or defaults that need checking before any code gets pasted anywhere.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What makes a PR disclosure like "parts of this code were AI-assisted, review with caution" — unchanged on every PR — disclosure theatre rather than real disclosure?

options.label: It's identical regardless of the PR's actual content, so it costs the reader nothing if removed
It mentions AI, which clients dislike seeing
It's too short to be useful

questions.explanation: The test for real disclosure is whether removing the sentence would cost the reader actual information. A boilerplate note true of every PR fails that test regardless of length or wording.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What should a genuinely useful PR disclosure specify?

options.label: What was generated versus hand-reasoned in this specific change, and where the author's confidence is lower
The exact AI model and version used
A generic caution appropriate to any AI-assisted PR

questions.explanation: This is what lets a reviewer allocate limited review time toward the parts that actually need it most — the change-specific confidence map, not a fixed sentence.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Why is "it reads cleanly and passes existing tests" a weak signal specifically for concurrency or security code?

options.label: Because those domains often need reasoning the reader can't do just by reading, and bugs there frequently don't show up in ordinary tests
Because concurrency code is always longer than other code
Because AI tools refuse to generate concurrency code

questions.explanation: Fluency and passing tests are decent general signals but specifically weak ones in domains where correctness depends on reasoning about cases ordinary tests and a normal read don't surface — race conditions being the clearest example.

questions.from: This module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: When a developer genuinely can't verify a piece of generated code is correct, what's the right move, per the module?

options.label: Ship it silently since it passes CI and looks reasonable
Name the gap explicitly so someone with the authority to accept the risk can decide, rather than letting silence decide by default
Refuse to ship anything until becoming an expert in the domain

questions.explanation: Refusing to falsely certify something as verified isn't refusing to help — it's making sure the decision to accept a real risk is made explicitly, by someone positioned to make it, instead of happening by default because nobody said anything.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Async by Default: Writing So Nobody Has to Ask
description: Writing a PR, a ticket update, or a Slack message so it answers the follow-up question before it gets asked — the actual skill behind working async well.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what makes a written update require no follow-up
Apply the anticipate-the-question standard to a real update

contentSections.title: The message that generates a reply

contentSections.body: "Pushed the fix, should be good to merge" gets a reply within the hour: "which fix, for which bug, and did you test the retry path?" Now there are two messages where one would have done, and the second one has to wait for someone to be awake.

contentSections.scenario: Two developers each finish a ticket and post an update in the team channel before logging off for the day. Developer A writes: "Fixed the checkout bug, ready for review." Developer B writes: "Fixed the checkout bug where a discount code applied twice on double-click — added a debounce on the apply button and a server-side idempotency check as backup. Tested: double-click no longer double-applies, single click still works, existing discount tests still pass. Didn't test: what happens if the idempotency check itself fails — flagging that as a possible follow-up if anyone has time. PR is up, ready for review."
contentSections.question: If both developers are now offline for eight hours, which update lets a reviewer actually start reviewing without waiting for either of them to wake up?

options.label: A's — it's shorter and gets to the point
B's — it answers what changed, why, what was tested, and what wasn't, without needing a reply
Neither — a reviewer always needs to ask the author questions regardless

feedback.a: Shortness isn't the same as completeness — A's update is short because it left out everything a reviewer would need: what the actual bug was, what the fix does, and what's been verified. A reviewer reading it has to either guess or wait eight hours for an answer.
feedback.b: Right. B's update isn't longer because B likes writing more — every extra sentence answers a specific question a reviewer would otherwise have had to ask and wait on: what broke, what the fix actually is, what's verified, and what isn't. That's the entire difference between async-friendly and async-blocking, and it has nothing to do with length for its own sake.
feedback.neither: Some questions are genuinely impossible to anticipate, but most of what blocks a reviewer isn't exotic — it's exactly the handful of things B's update answers up front: what changed, why, and what was checked. Anticipating the ordinary questions is most of the skill.

contentSections.concept: **A message written for async collaboration answers the questions a reader would otherwise have to ask and then wait on.** The length isn't the point — a longer message that still doesn't say what was tested is just as blocking as a short one. The test is whether a reader eight time zones and eight hours away can act on it without you.

contentSections.body: This matters more, not less, in AI-assisted work specifically, because the volume of change a person can produce in a day went up. A reviewer used to be able to infer a lot from watching someone work through a problem over a few hours in real time, or from a code's history of small, legible commits. A large AI-assisted diff that lands all at once, with a two-line description, removes that context entirely — the reviewer has nothing to go on but what was written down.
The test for an async update: can a reader eight hours away act on it without you? Length isn't the point — anticipating the questions is.

contentSections.title: The specific questions to answer in advance

contentSections.body: "Anticipate the questions" is easy to agree with and hard to do under deadline pressure, unless there's a short, concrete list of which questions actually recur.

contentSections.scenario: Reviewing what actually blocks reviewers across dozens of async PR threads, four kinds of questions come up constantly, and a handful of others rarely do.
contentSections.question: Which of these are the recurring questions worth answering pre-emptively in an AI-assisted PR specifically?

items.label: What was AI-generated versus hand-written or hand-modified, and where confidence is lower
What was actually tested, and — just as important — what wasn't
Why this approach, if there was an obvious alternative a reviewer might reasonably ask about
What editor theme or font the author used while working
What else this change touches or could affect, beyond the obvious files in the diff

explanation.what_generated: This is the accountability-module thread continuing here: telling a reviewer where confidence is already high versus where reasoning was novel lets them allocate review time well, and it's a question they'd otherwise have to ask.
explanation.what_tested: The single most common follow-up question on any PR, AI-assisted or not — and the AI-assisted version needs it more, because "looks complete" is a weaker signal than it used to be, per the accountability module's ownership standard.
explanation.why_approach: If there's a more obvious approach a reviewer would expect, silence on why it wasn't used invites exactly the round-trip question this lesson is about avoiding.
explanation.editor_theme: Irrelevant to whether the change is correct or reviewable — this doesn't belong in a PR description at all.
explanation.blast_radius: A change's effects outside the files literally touched — a shared utility, a downstream consumer of an API — is exactly the kind of thing a reviewer needs told rather than has to go discover themselves.

contentSections.synthesis: **Four questions, answered before they're asked: what was generated versus hand-reasoned, what was tested and what wasn't, why this approach over an obvious alternative, and what else this touches beyond the obvious diff.** Covering these four in a PR description or ticket update is most of what makes async collaboration actually work — it's a short, checkable list, not a vague instruction to "communicate well."

contentSections.body: Four recurring questions to answer before they're asked: what was generated, what was tested, why this approach, and what else this touches.

title: Getting Review When You're the Only One Who Understands It
description: What to do when you're the only person on the team who's spent real time in the part of the codebase an AI-assisted change touches.

learningObjectives.text: Structure a change so someone without domain context can meaningfully review it
Choose an appropriate review strategy when no qualified reviewer is available

contentSections.title: "Nobody else knows this code" is a solvable problem, sometimes

contentSections.body: A solo contractor generates a substantial refactor of the only payment-reconciliation module in a small company's codebase. There is, genuinely, no one else who has ever worked in this file. The PR sits unreviewed for four days, not because anyone's being negligent, but because nobody knows what "reviewed" would even mean here.

contentSections.problem: You're the only person with context on a generated change to the payment-reconciliation module. There's one other engineer on the team, competent generally but unfamiliar with this specific module and the accounting rules it encodes. How do you get a review that's actually worth something, instead of a rubber stamp?

steps.label: Separate what needs domain expertise from what doesn't
steps.work: Split the review into two questions: "is the code well-structured, tested, and free of obvious bugs" (a generalist can assess this) and "does this correctly implement the accounting rule for partial refunds" (this needs the domain knowledge only you currently have).
steps.why: Treating the whole review as one undifferentiated blob either wastes the generalist's time pretending to judge domain correctness they can't, or skips review entirely because "they wouldn't understand it anyway" — both are worse than splitting the two questions apart.

steps.label: Get the generalist to review what they can
steps.work: Ask the other engineer specifically to review structure, test coverage, and general code quality — and tell them explicitly that's the scope, so they're not guessing whether they're supposed to be judging the accounting logic too.
steps.why: A reviewer given an honest, bounded scope can do that scope well. A reviewer handed the whole thing with no scoping either freezes up or, worse, approves something they didn't actually evaluate because they assumed someone else would catch the parts they couldn't.

steps.label: Write out your own reasoning as if defending it to a skeptic
steps.work: For the domain-specific part, write a short document: here's the accounting rule as I understand it, here's how the code implements it, here's the specific test case that would fail if I had this wrong, here's what I'm least sure about.
steps.why: This is a real substitute for expert review, not a fake one — writing out your reasoning explicitly, in a form a future skeptical reader (including future-you) could check, catches a meaningful fraction of the errors a second expert would have caught, because most such errors are caught by being forced to state the reasoning plainly, not by someone else's brain specifically.

steps.label: Flag the residual risk explicitly, don't hide it
steps.work: In the PR itself, state plainly: "no one else on the team currently has deep context on the partial-refund accounting rule this touches — reviewed for structure and tests by [name], domain correctness verified by me alone with reasoning documented above. Flagging in case anyone with accounting background can sanity-check before this goes to production."
steps.why: This mirrors the accountability module's lesson on refusing work you can't verify: the answer isn't silence and it isn't blocking forever, it's naming the actual state of review honestly so whoever has authority over the risk can decide with real information.

faded.problem: A second case: you're the only person who understands a generated change to a custom rate-limiting algorithm for an internal API, and there is no one else at the company with distributed-systems background at all — not even a generalist who could review structure and tests meaningfully in this specific area.

blanks.prompt: Since even the generalist split from step 2 isn't available here, what's the fallback from step 3?
blanks.answer: write out your reasoning explicitly, as if defending it to a skeptic
accept: write it out for a future skeptical reader
blanks.why: When even a partial human reviewer isn't available, the documented-reasoning step becomes the primary review mechanism rather than a supplement to it — still real, just carrying more of the weight.

blanks.prompt: What should the PR say about the state of review here, following step 4's honesty principle?
blanks.answer: state plainly that no one else could review the domain-specific part, and what was done instead
accept: disclose that there was no qualified reviewer available
flag that this is self-reviewed with reasoning documented
blanks.why: The honesty is the same regardless of how thin the review actually was — naming it plainly is what lets anyone downstream, now or later, know exactly how much confidence this change actually earned.

blanks.prompt: Beyond documenting reasoning, name one additional safeguard worth adding specifically because no real second reviewer exists.
blanks.answer: extra monitoring or alerting on the affected system after it ships
blanks.why: When the review itself is thinner than usual, compensating with faster detection after shipping — monitoring, a staged rollout, an easy rollback — is a reasonable way to reduce the actual risk, not just document it.

contentSections.procedure: **Split what needs domain expertise from what doesn't, get whatever real review is available on the part that doesn't, document your own reasoning explicitly for the part that does, and disclose the actual state of review rather than letting a PR approval imply more confidence than really exists.** None of this fully replaces a second expert. All of it is real, and honest about what it is.

contentSections.body: Split domain-specific review from general review, document your reasoning explicitly where no expert exists, and disclose the real state of review rather than letting an approval imply more than it means.

contentSections.title: When to actually go find outside review

contentSections.body: Sometimes the honest answer isn't "document it and ship it with monitoring" — it's "this specific thing is worth paying for an outside expert to look at, even briefly."

contentSections.scenario: A solo developer is about to ship a generated change to how a system handles GDPR-relevant personal data deletion requests — a domain with real legal exposure if done wrong, and one they have no formal background in. A one-time paid consultation with a privacy-law-aware engineer costs roughly $300 for a focused, one-hour review.
contentSections.question: Given the accountability module's reasoning about when to refuse work you can't verify, is a $300, one-hour outside review a reasonable cost here relative to the risk of an undetected error in GDPR-relevant deletion logic shipping to production?
contentSections.unit: a yes/no judgment, expressed as a rough dollar comparison
contentSections.explanation: Yes, and the comparison is what makes it obvious: $300 is a trivial cost next to the plausible downside of a GDPR compliance failure, which can run into real regulatory exposure and reputational damage that dwarfs a one-hour consulting fee many times over. This is exactly the situation the accountability module's "refuse work you can't review" lesson pointed toward without fully resolving — sometimes the answer to "I can't verify this" isn't a workaround at all, it's spending a small, known cost to convert an unverifiable risk into a verified one. The mistake isn't spending the $300; it's not even considering the option because self-review felt like the only path available.

contentSections.body: Outside review is worth it when three things are true together: the domain genuinely requires expertise nobody in-house has, the consequence of being wrong is disproportionate to the cost of checking, and the check itself is cheap and fast relative to that consequence. GDPR-adjacent logic, security-critical authentication changes, and anything with direct financial-reporting implications tend to clear that bar. A cosmetic feature or an internal tool usually doesn't — not because outside review is never worth it there, but because the consequence side of the comparison is much smaller.
Outside review is worth paying for when expertise is genuinely missing in-house, the cost of being wrong is disproportionate, and the check itself is cheap relative to that risk.

title: Disagreeing About Generated Code Without Relitigating the Tool
description: Keeping a disagreement about a specific piece of generated code from turning into a repeated argument about whether AI tools should be used at all.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a disagreement about a specific change from a disagreement about tool policy
Redirect a tool-policy argument back to the specific, resolvable disagreement

contentSections.title: Two different arguments wearing the same words

contentSections.body: "I don't think this approach is right" and "I don't think we should be using AI for this kind of code at all" can come out of the same reviewer's mouth, in the same comment thread, about the same PR — and only one of them is about this PR.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer comments on a generated PR: "This validation logic misses the case where the input is an empty string but not null — and honestly, this is why I'm skeptical of leaning on AI for anything touching input validation." The thread that follows spends forty minutes debating whether AI-generated code is trustworthy in general, and the empty-string bug is still unfixed at the end of it.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that let a specific, fixable bug turn into an unresolved forty-minute policy debate?

options.label: The reviewer was wrong about the bug, so the conversation correctly moved to a bigger question

The comment bundled a specific, checkable claim (the empty-string case) with a general, unfalsifiable one (skepticism about AI for validation broadly), and the reply engaged with the second instead of the first
Forty minutes is a normal and appropriate amount of time for any code review disagreement

feedback.wrong_bug: The bug appears to be real and specific — nothing suggests the reviewer was wrong about it. The problem isn't that the conversation moved because the specific claim was false; it's that it moved even though the specific claim was fixable and separate from the general one.
feedback.bundled: This is the mechanism: a specific, resolvable claim (this exact case is missing) got bundled with a general, much harder to resolve one (should we trust AI-generated validation code as a category), in the same sentence. Once the reply engaged with the general claim, the specific one — the actual thing blocking the merge — got lost in a debate that was never going to end in forty minutes anyway.
feedback.normal: Forty minutes spent resolving a specific missing-edge-case bug would be unusual and probably too long for something this bounded. Forty minutes spent on an unresolvable general policy question, when a two-line fix was sitting right there, is the actual failure — not the time itself, but what it was spent on.

contentSections.mechanism: **A specific bug and a general skepticism about the category of work are two different claims, and only one of them can actually be resolved in a PR thread.** The fix isn't ignoring the general point — it's separating it out loud: fix the specific, checkable thing now, and if the general skepticism is worth having, have it deliberately, somewhere else, as its own conversation with its own outcome — not as a detour inside a comment thread that was supposed to be about one bug.

contentSections.body: A specific bug and a general skepticism about AI-generated code are different claims. Fix the specific one now; have the general debate deliberately, elsewhere, if it's worth having at all.

contentSections.title: Redirecting without dismissing

contentSections.body: The move that works isn't "let's not talk about that here," which reads as shutting the reviewer down. It's separating the two things out loud, in a way that takes both seriously.

contentSections.code: PR comment reply: "That's not really relevant to this PR, can we stick to the actual bug please."
contentSections.question: This reply correctly identifies that the conversation drifted into general AI skepticism. What's the flaw in how it handles that?

options.label: It dismisses the reviewer's broader concern outright instead of acknowledging it and giving it somewhere to go
It's too long and should be shorter
It doesn't apologize enough for the bug existing

feedback.dismiss: Right. Being correct that the general point doesn't belong in this thread doesn't mean the general point is wrong or unworthy of discussion — dismissing it outright, with no acknowledgment, reads as defensive and is likely to make the reviewer raise it again, louder, next time, since it was never actually heard.
feedback.long: Length isn't the problem — a short reply that dismisses a real concern is still a worse reply than a slightly longer one that separates the two claims respectfully.
feedback.apologize: An apology for the bug isn't really what's needed or what's missing here — the missing piece is acknowledging the broader concern exists and deserves a real conversation, just not this one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix keeps both claims alive but in the right place: "Good catch on the empty-string case, fixing that now. On the broader question of how much we lean on AI for validation logic — that's a real conversation worth having, but I don't think we should decide it inside this PR thread. Want to raise it at the next team sync, or should I open a separate discussion?" This takes the general concern seriously enough to give it a real venue, instead of either derailing the PR into it or dismissing it as if it doesn't matter.

contentSections.body: Separate the two claims respectfully: fix the specific bug now, and give the general concern a real venue instead of dismissing it or letting it derail the PR.

title: Being the Person Who Can't Take a Call Today
description: Handling a synchronous request — a meeting, a call, a "can you hop on for five minutes" — when today genuinely isn't a day you can do that, without it costing you standing on the team.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a synchronous request into a workable async alternative
Decline a call in a way that preserves trust and doesn't over-explain

contentSections.title: The request that assumes today is a normal day

contentSections.body: "Can you hop on a quick call to walk me through this PR?" is a completely reasonable ask on a completely reasonable day. On a day where a call costs three times what it looks like it costs, it's a request built on an assumption that happens to be wrong today, and nobody sending it could have known that.

contentSections.scenario: A teammate asks in Slack: "hey can you jump on a call for 5 min, I'm confused about the retry logic in your PR." It's a genuinely low-capacity day. Three possible replies: (1) accept the call anyway and push through it, (2) reply "can't today, sorry" and nothing else, (3) reply "can't do a call today, but let me write up the retry logic here — give me 15 minutes and I'll have a clear explanation with the specific lines called out."
contentSections.question: Which reply actually serves both people — the teammate who needs the answer, and the reality of the day?

options.label: Option 1 — pushing through keeps the team moving fastest
Option 3 — it declines the call specifically while still delivering the actual thing the teammate needed
Option 2 — a short, honest no is enough on its own

feedback.opt1: Pushing through on a day a call costs triple doesn't actually keep the team moving fastest — it risks a worse outcome now (a foggy, harder-to-follow explanation) and a worse tomorrow (the actual cost of pushing through catches up later). The team isn't served by an explanation given at reduced capacity that has to be redone anyway.
feedback.opt3: Right. This declines the specific thing that's actually expensive today — the synchronous call — while still delivering what the teammate needed, in a form (written, at your own pace) that fits the day. Nobody's blocked, and nothing about today's reality had to be explained or justified to get there.
feedback.opt2: A short no is honest and reasonable, and it's still incomplete — it leaves the teammate's actual question unanswered and, quietly, leaves them to wonder whether to ask again, ask someone else, or just wait. Pairing the no with a concrete alternative removes that ambiguity.

contentSections.concept: **Declining the synchronous form of a request while still delivering the substance is almost always available, and it's the move that costs the least on both sides.** The call wasn't actually what the teammate needed — an answer was. Most requests that arrive as "can we hop on a call" are really "I need X," and X is very often deliverable async, at lower cost, without the day's reality ever needing to become the topic of conversation.

contentSections.body: This is a specific instance of a broader move worth having ready: separate the *form* of a request from its *substance*. A stand-up update, a pairing session, a walkthrough call — these are all forms. The substance underneath is usually something narrower and more deliverable async: a status, an explanation, a decision. Substituting a written, asynchronous version of the substance, offered clearly and without apology, is available far more often than it feels like it is under the pressure of a live "can you hop on" message.
Most "can we hop on a call" requests are really "I need X." Deliver X in writing, at your own pace, and the call was never actually necessary.

contentSections.title: Saying no without over-explaining

contentSections.body: There's a version of declining that turns into a paragraph justifying why, medically or personally, today is hard. It's honest, and it's more than the situation calls for — and it's worth knowing the shorter version that still works.

contentSections.intro: A manager messages: "quick sync in 10 to go over the sprint plan?" on a day that genuinely isn't a call day. Build the reply.

fields.prompt: How should the decline itself be framed?
options: A detailed explanation of the health reason a call isn't possible today
A brief, factual statement — "can't do a live call today" — with no justification required
An open-ended "maybe later" that doesn't actually decline
fields.correctValue: A brief, factual statement — "can't do a live call today" — with no justification required
fields.feedback: This mirrors the reviewer-profile and scoping lessons earlier in the track: state the constraint as fact, not as an apology or a medical explanation nobody asked for and that isn't actually the manager's business to manage.

fields.prompt: What should come immediately after the decline?
options: Nothing — the decline stands alone
A concrete async alternative: what you can deliver, and roughly when
A promise to reschedule as soon as you're feeling better
fields.correctValue: A concrete async alternative: what you can deliver, and roughly when
fields.feedback: Without this, a brief decline can read as unhelpful even when it isn't meant that way. Pairing it with a specific alternative — "I can write up the sprint plan and comments by end of day" — shows the substance is still coming, just not in that form.

fields.prompt: What tone should the whole message carry?
options: Apologetic throughout, expressing regret for the inconvenience
Matter-of-fact — stating the constraint and the plan the same way you'd state any other scheduling fact
Defensive, pre-empting any pushback
fields.correctValue: Matter-of-fact — stating the constraint and the plan the same way you'd state any other scheduling fact
fields.feedback: Apology and defensiveness both frame the constraint as something to justify or brace for pushback on. Matter-of-fact framing treats it as an ordinary scheduling fact, which is what it is — and tends to be met in kind, precisely because it isn't presented as something requiring debate.

contentSections.synthesis: Put together: "Can't do a live call today, but I'll have written notes on the sprint plan with my input by end of day — happy to jump on async in the thread if anything needs back-and-forth." One sentence declining, one sentence with the concrete alternative, both stated as fact. Nothing here requires the manager to know why, and nothing here leaves the actual need unmet.

contentSections.body: State the constraint as fact, pair it with a concrete async alternative, keep the tone matter-of-fact — no apology and no explanation owed.

title: Building a Review Habit When There's No Reviewer
description: A concrete self-review procedure for the days — or the whole career stretch — when there's no second person to catch what you missed.

learningObjectives.text: Design a repeatable self-review procedure for AI-assisted changes
Apply the procedure to a change as if reviewing a stranger's work

contentSections.title: Why self-review usually fails, and the specific fix

contentSections.body: "I reviewed my own code before merging" is true of almost everyone and catches almost nothing, most of the time — not because people are careless, but because the part of your brain that just wrote or approved something is the worst-positioned part of your brain to doubt it.

contentSections.scenario: A solo developer re-reads their own generated PR before merging, finds it looks fine, merges it, and a bug ships that a colleague would likely have caught in thirty seconds of review. This has happened to them more than once, despite genuinely trying to review carefully each time.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely reason self-review keeps missing things a fresh reviewer wouldn't?

options.label: The developer isn't trying hard enough

Re-reading your own recent reasoning tends to confirm it rather than challenge it — the mental state of self-review is fundamentally different from the mental state of reviewing someone else's unfamiliar work
Self-review is impossible and shouldn't be attempted at all

feedback.effort: The developer describes genuinely trying — the pattern shows up despite real effort, which points away from an effort problem and toward something structural about the activity itself.
feedback.confirmation: This is the real mechanism, and it's well-documented outside coding too: a person checking their own recent reasoning tends to re-experience it as reasonable, because it's the same mental path they just walked, not a fresh one. A second person reviewing has no attachment to the reasoning and no memory of how it felt correct in the moment — that's precisely what makes an outside review catch things self-review doesn't.
feedback.impossible: Self-review clearly isn't worthless — it catches plenty. The lesson isn't that it's useless, it's that it needs a specific structural fix to compensate for the confirmation problem, which is exactly what the rest of this lesson provides.

contentSections.mechanism: **Self-review's weakness isn't effort — it's that re-reading your own reasoning tends to confirm it, because you're retracing a path you already walked, not encountering something fresh.** The fix isn't trying harder at the same activity; it's changing the activity itself into something that doesn't have that structural advantage for the reasoning that's already there.

contentSections.body: Self-review's weakness is structural, not a lack of effort — re-reading your own reasoning tends to confirm it. The fix has to change the activity, not the effort.

contentSections.title: A procedure that doesn't rely on rereading your own reasoning

contentSections.body: The fix mirrors what a second reviewer actually does differently: they come at the code cold, without the context of having just written or approved it. A procedure can force something close to that, alone.

contentSections.intro: Design a self-review procedure that doesn't rely on rereading your own fresh reasoning — build it from the pieces below.

fields.prompt: What should happen between finishing the change and reviewing it?
options: Review immediately, while the reasoning is freshest
Put a real gap in — even twenty minutes on something else, ideally longer — before reviewing
No gap needed if you're focused enough
fields.correctValue: Put a real gap in — even twenty minutes on something else, ideally longer — before reviewing
fields.feedback: This directly targets the confirmation mechanism: a gap, even a short one, breaks the sense of "I just walked this path and it felt right," and lets you approach the diff slightly more like a stranger would.

fields.prompt: What question should frame the review, instead of "does this look right"?
options: "Does this look right?"
"What would make this wrong, and did I check for it?" — actively hunting for the failure mode, not confirming the success
"Would I be embarrassed if someone saw this?"
fields.correctValue: "What would make this wrong, and did I check for it?" — actively hunting for the failure mode, not confirming the success
fields.feedback: "Does this look right" invites the same confirming read that caused the problem. "What would make this wrong" forces an adversarial stance toward your own work, which is closer to what a genuine second reviewer brings by default.

fields.prompt: What should the review actually check against, to avoid relying purely on memory of what matters?
options: A short, written, standing checklist — edge cases, what was tested, what wasn't, blast radius — used the same way every time
Whatever comes to mind in the moment
The same four questions from lesson one's async-writing checklist, since they were about something else
fields.correctValue: A short, written, standing checklist — edge cases, what was tested, what wasn't, blast radius — used the same way every time
fields.feedback: A written, standing checklist doesn't rely on remembering what to check under time pressure — it's exactly the kind of external structure that compensates for a mental state (self-review) that's naturally biased toward confirming rather than doubting.

fields.prompt: What should come out of the review, even when working completely alone?
options: Nothing written — just a decision to merge or not
A short written note: what was checked, what was found, what's still uncertain — even if no one else will read it today
A verbal summary to yourself
fields.correctValue: A short written note: what was checked, what was found, what's still uncertain — even if no one else will read it today
fields.feedback: Writing it down, even for an audience of nobody today, is what the accountability module's disclosure lessons were building toward — it exists for future-you, for a teammate who joins later, and for the version of this habit that becomes real disclosure the moment anyone else is on the project.

contentSections.synthesis: **A gap before reviewing, a review framed as hunting for the failure mode rather than confirming success, a standing written checklist instead of memory, and a written artifact even when no one else will read it today.** None of this fully replaces a second person — nothing does — but all four pieces specifically target the structural reason self-review fails, rather than just asking for more effort at the same flawed activity.

contentSections.body: A real gap before reviewing, hunting for the failure mode instead of confirming success, a standing checklist, and a written artifact — that's a self-review habit built to compensate for what self-review structurally can't do.

title: Practice — Rewrite Seven Synchronous Asks as Async Ones
description: Seven drills across async communication, review-without-a-reviewer, and self-review. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's async and review standards to unfamiliar situations
Convert a synchronous request into a workable async form at speed

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven situations, each needing an async-friendly rewrite or a review-strategy decision. Do them in one sitting or three.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint.

title: Lab — Run a Full Change Through Async-Only Collaboration
description: Take a real or realistic change from brief to shipped using only written, asynchronous communication — no calls, no synchronous pairing — and produce a record where every decision is written down.

learningObjectives.text: Run a real change through fully asynchronous collaboration
Produce a written change record that requires no meeting to understand

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This lab is a constraint exercise: take one real or realistic change from request to shipped, using only written communication throughout, and produce a record that proves it — a trail where every decision is legible to someone who wasn't there.

contentSections.title: An async-only change, start to finish
contentSections.brief: Pick one bounded, real (or realistically simulated) change — a bug fix, a small feature, a refactor. Run it entirely in writing: the initial brief, any clarifying questions, the implementation notes, the self-review, and the final write-up. If you have a real collaborator willing to play reviewer async, use them; if not, write the reviewer's likely questions and your answers yourself, honestly, as if a stranger were asking.
contentSections.deliverable: A change record — brief, clarifying Q&A, implementation notes following lesson one's four-question standard, a self-review using lesson five's procedure, and a final summary — where nothing required a call or a meeting to understand.

stages.title: Write the brief as received (or write it yourself, realistically)
stages.instructions: State the task as it would actually arrive — the situation, not a cleaned-up spec. If simulating, write it the way a real, slightly ambiguous request would sound.
stages.checkpoint: The brief reads like a real request, ambiguity included, not an idealized spec.

stages.title: Ask and answer the clarifying questions in writing
stages.instructions: List the real unknowns (per the estimating module's evidence-stack pattern) and answer them in writing, as if async with whoever gave the brief — no live conversation, even if simulated.
stages.checkpoint: At least one real unknown is named and resolved on the page, not assumed silently.

stages.title: Do the work and write the implementation notes
stages.instructions: Make the change. Write it up using lesson one's four questions: what was generated versus hand-reasoned, what was tested and what wasn't, why this approach, what else this touches.
stages.checkpoint: All four questions are answered specifically, not generically.

stages.title: Run the lesson-five self-review procedure
stages.instructions: Take a real gap (even a short break), then review using "what would make this wrong" framing against a written checklist, and write the resulting note — what was checked, what was found, what's still uncertain.
stages.checkpoint: A written self-review note exists, separate from the implementation notes, showing the failure-mode framing.

stages.title: Write the final summary
stages.instructions: One paragraph a reviewer (real or imagined) could read cold and know exactly what happened, why, and what to check — closing the loop on the whole async trail.
stages.checkpoint: The summary alone, read with nothing else, tells a stranger what they need to know.

rubric.criterion: The brief is realistic, not idealized
rubric.meets: Reads like an actual request, ambiguity and all — not a cleaned-up spec written after the fact.

rubric.criterion: At least one real unknown is resolved in writing
rubric.meets: A genuine unknown appears and gets answered on the page, not silently assumed.

rubric.criterion: Implementation notes answer all four of lesson one's questions
rubric.meets: Generated-vs-hand-reasoned, tested-vs-not, why this approach, and blast radius are each answered specifically.

rubric.criterion: The self-review uses the failure-mode framing, not a confirming read
rubric.meets: The written note shows evidence of hunting for what would make it wrong, not just noting that it looks fine.

rubric.criterion: The whole record needs no meeting to understand
rubric.meets: A stranger reading only the written trail — no verbal context — could follow what happened and why.

contentSections.body: A change record this complete is what makes async collaboration a real substitute for a meeting, not a weaker version of one — a stranger reading it cold has everything a meeting would have given them, on their own schedule.

title: Checkpoint — Working With a Team, and Without One
description: Ten questions, 40% this module, 40% the previous module (Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure), 20% from module one (Estimating and Scoping).

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and reconnect them to the phase's earlier modules

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Working With a Team, and Without One
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four from Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure, two from Estimating and Scoping.

questions.from: This module — Working With a Team, and Without One
questions.prompt: What makes an async update actually useful, per lesson one?

options.label: Whether it answers the questions a reader would otherwise have to ask and wait on
How short it is
Whether it's posted in the right channel

questions.explanation: Length isn't the test — a short update that leaves out what was tested is just as blocking as a long one that does. The test is whether a reader far away in time can act on it alone.

questions.from: This module — Working With a Team, and Without One
questions.prompt: When you're the only person who understands a piece of domain-specific generated code, what's the recommended approach?

options.label: Split domain-specific review from general review, document your own reasoning explicitly, and disclose the real state of review
Ship it without review, since no one else can review it anyway
Block indefinitely until an expert becomes available

questions.explanation: A generalist can still review structure and tests; the domain-specific part gets your own documented reasoning; and the PR should say plainly what was and wasn't actually reviewed, rather than letting an approval imply more confidence than exists.

questions.from: This module — Working With a Team, and Without One
questions.prompt: A reviewer bundles a specific missing-edge-case bug with general skepticism about AI-generated code in one comment. What's the right move?

options.label: Separate the two: fix the specific bug now, give the general concern a real venue elsewhere
Dismiss the general concern as irrelevant to this PR
Debate the general question fully before touching the specific bug

questions.explanation: A specific bug and a general policy question are different claims; only the specific one is resolvable in this thread. Dismissing the general concern outright reads as defensive; letting it derail the PR leaves the actual bug unfixed.

questions.from: This module — Working With a Team, and Without One
questions.prompt: Why does self-review structurally miss things a fresh reviewer catches?

options.label: Re-reading your own recent reasoning tends to confirm it rather than challenge it
People reviewing their own code simply don't try hard enough
Self-review is only a problem for AI-generated code specifically

questions.explanation: The mechanism is structural, not about effort: retracing reasoning you just walked tends to feel reasonable again, unlike a fresh reviewer encountering it cold — which is why the fix has to change the activity, not just try harder at it.

questions.from: Previous module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Who is accountable when AI-generated code ships a bug that review missed?

options.label: The developer who merged it
The AI tool
No one specifically

questions.explanation: Merging is authorship regardless of how the code was produced — a tool has no standing to be accountable, so responsibility lands with whoever approved and shipped it.

questions.from: Previous module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What makes a PR disclosure real rather than theatre?

options.label: It's specific to this change — removing it would cost the reader actual information
It mentions the word "AI" somewhere
It's included on every PR without exception

questions.explanation: A fixed, boilerplate note true of every PR fails the theatre test; a note specific to this diff, naming what's generated versus hand-reasoned and where confidence is lower, passes it.

questions.from: Previous module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What kind of generated-code risk has no distinctive string to search for and is caught only by domain expertise?

options.label: An outdated or insecure-but-plausible pattern, like a weak hashing algorithm
A verbatim match to a licensed open-source repository
Any function longer than 40 lines

questions.explanation: License risk is searchable via a distinctive string; currency/domain risk runs without error and looks fine on a skim, caught only by someone who knows the domain well enough to recognize it.

questions.from: Previous module — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: When a developer genuinely can't verify a piece of generated code, what's the recommended response?

options.label: Name the gap explicitly so someone with authority to accept the risk can decide
Ship it quietly since it passes CI
Refuse all further work until becoming an expert

questions.explanation: Refusing to falsely certify something as verified isn't refusing to help — it makes sure the risk-acceptance decision is made explicitly by someone positioned to make it, not by default through silence.

questions.from: Two modules back — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: What does AI generation speed actually shorten?

options.label: Mainly the generation step itself, not review or integration
The whole job, roughly proportionally
Nothing measurable

questions.explanation: Review time is set by how much trust the result needs, which doesn't shrink just because typing got faster.

questions.from: Two modules back — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: Why is a client-facing estimate range like "5–7 days" bad if it doesn't name what the range depends on?

options.label: The client can't act on unexplained uncertainty — a named variable turns it into a decision they can make
Ranges are inherently unprofessional and should never be used
It should always be the higher number to be safe

questions.explanation: A range with no named cause is a hedge, not information. Naming what it depends on — and ideally how to find out fast — turns it into something the client can actually use.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: What a Working Day of Tool Use Actually Costs
description: Adding up the real cost of a day of AI-assisted work — subscription, token usage, and the time spent managing the tool itself — instead of the number that sits quietly on a monthly statement.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the full set of costs a day of AI tool use actually carries
Compare a tool's advertised price to its real per-working-day cost

contentSections.title: The number on the pricing page isn't the number

contentSections.body: "$20 a month" sounds like the cost of an AI coding subscription. Then there's a second tool for a specific task the first one doesn't handle well, a usage-based API charge that spiked during a big refactor week, and the twenty minutes lost this morning working around a rate limit mid-task. None of that was on the pricing page.

contentSections.scenario: A freelancer tallies a typical month: a $20/month subscription to a coding assistant, a separate $15/month subscription to a different tool used for a specific documentation-generation task, roughly $40 in pay-as-you-go API usage during a heavy week, and — unlogged, unbilled, easy to miss — about ninety minutes total across the month spent working around rate limits, outages, or switching between tools when one underperformed on a task.
contentSections.question: What's the most accurate description of "what this month of AI tooling cost"?

options.label: $20 — the headline subscription price, since that's the main tool
$75 — the sum of all the money actually spent across subscriptions and usage
$75 plus the value of roughly ninety minutes of otherwise-billable or otherwise-usable time lost to friction

feedback.headline: The headline price is what gets remembered and budgeted around, but it's less than a third of what actually left the account this month, before even counting time.
feedback.money_sum: $75 is the real cash total, and it's still an undercount — ninety minutes of a working month is real cost too, whether it shows up as lost billable time for a freelancer or lost focus time for anyone else. Money spent and time spent are both real costs; counting only one systematically underestimates the true figure.
feedback.full: This is the complete picture: cash costs across every tool actually used, plus the time cost of friction — rate limits, outages, tool-switching — which doesn't appear on any invoice but is just as real a cost of the day. A freelancer billing by the hour can literally price the ninety minutes; anyone else can still recognize it as ninety minutes not spent on the actual work.

contentSections.concept: **The real cost of a day of AI-assisted work is every tool actually used, at actual usage-based rates, plus the time lost to the tool's own friction — not the headline price of the main subscription.** Budgeting around the headline number is how a $20/month tool quietly becomes a $75-plus-ninety-minutes month, discovered only when someone finally adds it up.

contentSections.body: This matters for the same reason review-time estimating mattered in the first module of this phase: a number that looks small and precise ("$20/month") invites treating the tool as close to free, which changes decisions — using it for tasks where it's marginal, not questioning a second subscription, not noticing that friction time has crept up. A number built from the real total invites the opposite: asking, occasionally, whether the actual cost still buys what it used to.
The real monthly cost is every tool actually used at real rates, plus time lost to friction — not the one subscription price that gets remembered.

contentSections.title: Building the real number

contentSections.body: Turning "it's probably more than the subscription" into an actual number takes about fifteen minutes, once a month, and changes what "is this tool worth it" even means.

contentSections.scenario: A developer tracks their AI tool usage for one representative week: a flat subscription prorated to about $5 for the week, $18 in pay-as-you-go API charges for a token-heavy refactoring task, and — timed honestly, with a stopwatch, out of curiosity — 35 minutes total spent on rate-limit waits, a short outage, and re-prompting after a confusing tool response.
contentSections.question: If this developer values their own working time at a conservative $40/hour, what's the total real cost of that week's AI tool use, in dollars — cash plus time, rounded to the nearest 5?
contentSections.explanation: $5 + $18 = $23 in cash, and 35 minutes at $40/hour is about $23.30 more — total close to $45, roughly double the cash figure alone. This is a useful habit specifically because the ratio, not just the absolute number, is informative: friction time here cost almost as much as the money did, which is easy to miss entirely if only the invoice gets checked. A month where friction time genuinely doubles the cash cost is a month where fixing the friction — a better prompt habit, a different tool, a workaround for a specific rate limit — is worth real attention, and that's invisible until the time gets counted at all.

contentSections.body: This doesn't need to be a permanent habit — a rough one-week tally, done honestly with a timer for the friction part, once every few months or whenever a tool's pricing or behavior changes, is enough to keep the mental model accurate. The goal isn't precision to the cent. It's catching the moment a tool's real cost has quietly drifted from what's still budgeted for it in your head.
A rough weekly tally — cash plus honestly-timed friction — done occasionally is enough to catch a tool's real cost drifting from what's still assumed about it.

title: Rate Limits, Outages, and the Deadline That Doesn't Move
description: Planning for the specific, predictable ways an AI tool becomes unavailable mid-task, so a deadline doesn't quietly depend on a tool having a perfect day.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the predictable failure modes of an AI tool during a working day
Build a contingency plan that survives a tool being unavailable at the worst moment

contentSections.title: The outage always seems to land on the bad day

contentSections.body: It's not actually more likely to happen on a deadline day. It just costs the most, and gets remembered the most, when it does — a provider's API goes down for forty minutes, right in the middle of finishing a change due in two hours.

contentSections.problem: You're two hours from a client deadline, mid-task, relying on an AI coding tool for a chunk of remaining work, when the provider's API starts returning errors. Build a plan for this specific situation, in advance — before it happens, not while it's happening.

steps.label: Name the specific failure modes worth planning for
steps.work: Three recurring ones: a full outage (nothing responds), a rate limit (responds, but throttled or blocked after heavy use), and a degraded response (responds, but slower or lower quality than usual, harder to notice in the moment).
steps.why: Vague dread ("what if the tool breaks") doesn't produce a plan. Three specific, recurring failure modes do, because each one has a different signature and a different appropriate response.

steps.label: Decide, per failure mode, what the fallback actually is
steps.work: Full outage: switch immediately to doing the remaining work by hand, even if slower — don't wait and hope it comes back. Rate limit: slow down request frequency, batch remaining questions into fewer, larger prompts. Degraded response: fall back to more manual verification of anything it does produce, since "looks a bit off" is a real, if fuzzy, signal.
steps.why: Each failure mode has a genuinely different right response — waiting is sometimes correct for a rate limit (it usually resets soon) and almost never correct for a full outage with a fixed deadline two hours out.

steps.label: Pre-identify what work is realistic to finish by hand in the time left
steps.work: Before any outage happens, have a rough sense of which parts of a typical task are fast to do by hand (a small config change, a straightforward function) and which genuinely depend on the tool's speed (a large boilerplate-heavy scaffold). If an outage hits with two hours left, the by-hand-feasible parts get triaged first.
steps.why: This triage is much faster and more accurate done calmly in advance than improvised under the stress of a ticking deadline and a broken tool at the same time.

steps.label: Decide the deadline-communication trigger in advance
steps.work: Set a private rule: if the outage or degradation isn't resolved within some fixed window (say, 15 minutes), stop waiting and message the client immediately with the situation and a revised plan — echoing the renegotiation-timing lesson from the estimating module.
steps.why: Deciding the trigger in advance, as a fixed rule, removes the temptation to keep hoping "just five more minutes" past the point where disclosing early would have mattered — the same early-signal principle from renegotiating a blown estimate.

faded.problem: A second case: you're relying on an AI tool for a substantial data-transformation script, four hours from a deadline, and the tool starts returning noticeably worse output — plausible-looking but subtly wrong in ways you're catching on review, roughly one error in every three responses instead of the usual one in ten.

blanks.prompt: Which of the three failure modes is this — outage, rate limit, or degraded response?
blanks.answer: degraded response
blanks.why: It's still responding, and not being throttled — it's just producing worse output than usual, which is the hardest of the three to notice because nothing errors out.

blanks.prompt: What's the appropriate fallback from step 2 for this specific failure mode?
blanks.answer: fall back to more manual verification of anything it produces
blanks.why: Since the tool is still responding, the useful response isn't switching away entirely — it's trusting its output less and checking more, since the signal (higher error rate) is real even though it's fuzzy.

blanks.prompt: Given four hours left and a noticeably higher error rate, what should the private deadline-communication trigger be checking for?
blanks.answer: whether the extra verification time itself is eating into the four hours enough to put the deadline at risk
accept: whether verification is slowing things down enough to threaten the deadline
if the extra review time risks the deadline
blanks.why: Degraded-response failures are sneaky because they don't stop the work, they slow it down through extra verification — the trigger has to track that slowdown against the remaining time, not just watch for a hard failure.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the specific failure modes in advance — outage, rate limit, degraded response — decide the fallback for each before it's needed, pre-identify what's realistic to finish by hand, and set a fixed, private trigger for when to stop waiting and communicate.** All of this is easy to reason about calmly in advance and hard to improvise well while a deadline is actively ticking down.

contentSections.body: Outage, rate limit, and degraded response are three different failure modes with three different right responses — decide all three, and the deadline-disclosure trigger, before any of them happen.

contentSections.title: Building the habit of noticing degradation

contentSections.body: A full outage announces itself. Degraded quality doesn't — it just quietly costs more review time until something finally slips through.

contentSections.scenario: A developer is deciding which signals are actually worth treating as "the tool might be degraded right now" versus normal day-to-day variation.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine signals worth noticing, as opposed to noise?

items.label: Catching noticeably more errors in generated output than usual, across several consecutive requests
Response times that are consistently much slower than the tool's normal range, not just one slow request
One single response that turned out to be wrong
A vague sense that today "feels off" with no specific evidence
The provider's own status page or community reports of a known incident

explanation.error_rate: A pattern across several consecutive requests, not one, is a real signal — this is what separates "the tool made a mistake, which happens" from "something is actually different right now."
explanation.response_time: Same logic — a consistent shift from the normal range, not a single slow response (which could be a hundred ordinary things), is worth acting on.
explanation.single_miss: Any tool is wrong sometimes even on a completely normal day — that's what the correctness-review habit from the estimating module already assumes and accounts for. A single miss isn't evidence of degradation, it's the baseline error rate the review process exists to catch.
explanation.vague_feeling: A hunch with no specific evidence isn't a signal to act on directly, though it's worth noticing as a prompt to actually check for the real signals — error rate, response time, status page — rather than acting on the feeling itself.
explanation.provider_status: An external, independent confirmation is one of the strongest signals available and worth checking the moment a pattern (not a single miss) is noticed.

contentSections.synthesis: **A pattern across multiple requests — not one miss, not a vague feeling — plus an external check of the provider's status, is what separates a real degradation signal from ordinary day-to-day noise.** Treating every single wrong answer as "the tool is degraded today" would be exhausting and mostly wrong; treating a real pattern as just bad luck is how the fallback plan from lesson two never actually gets triggered when it should.

contentSections.body: A pattern across several requests, plus an independent status check, is a real degradation signal. A single miss or a vague feeling isn't — that's ordinary variation the review process already accounts for.

title: Keeping the Skill You'd Need Without the Tool
description: Deciding, deliberately, which underlying skills need active maintenance even though the tool makes them rarely necessary day to day — before a gap in that skill becomes the emergency.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which underlying skills are at real risk of atrophy from tool reliance
Choose a low-cost way to maintain a skill that's rarely exercised directly

contentSections.title: The skill you didn't notice going quiet

contentSections.body: A developer who used to write regular expressions from memory realizes, mid-outage, that they now can't quite remember the syntax for a non-greedy match without looking it up or asking a tool — not because they got worse at the underlying logic, but because the tool has been doing that specific, small thing for over a year without them noticing the muscle going quiet.

contentSections.scenario: A developer notices, during an unrelated outage, that several small skills — writing a regex from scratch, recalling a specific standard-library function's exact signature, debugging without an AI tool's suggestions — feel noticeably rustier than they remember, even though bigger-picture skills like system design and reading someone else's code feel completely unaffected.
contentSections.question: What best explains why some skills atrophied and others didn't, given the same period of heavy tool use?

options.label: The tool made this developer generally worse at programming
The skills that atrophied are specifically the small, frequent, mechanical ones the tool now handles routinely — the skills the tool doesn't touch stayed exercised
This is random and not actually predictable

feedback.general: System design and code-reading — arguably harder skills — stayed sharp, which rules out a general decline. Something more specific is going on.
feedback.specific: This is the pattern: skill atrophy tracks specifically with what got delegated, not with overall skill level. Small, mechanical, frequently-needed tasks (regex syntax, a function signature) got handled by the tool so routinely that the underlying recall muscle went unused — while skills the tool was never doing (architectural judgment, reading unfamiliar code) kept getting exercised the whole time, because nothing replaced the need to do them.
feedback.random: It's not random — it's predictable from exactly which tasks got delegated most heavily and most routinely. That predictability is what makes it possible to decide, in advance, which skills need deliberate maintenance rather than discovering the gap during an actual emergency.

contentSections.mechanism: **Skill atrophy tracks with delegation, not with tool use in general — the specific things a tool handles routinely are the specific things that go rusty, while everything the tool doesn't touch stays exercised by ordinary use.** This makes the risk identifiable in advance: look at what gets delegated most routinely and most completely, and that's the shortlist of skills worth deliberately maintaining.

contentSections.body: Skill atrophy tracks with what's delegated most routinely, not with tool use overall — which makes the at-risk skills identifiable in advance, not just discoverable in an emergency.

contentSections.title: Deciding what's worth actively maintaining

contentSections.body: Not every delegated skill is worth actively maintaining — that would be its own kind of wasted effort. The question is which ones, and a specific test answers it.

contentSections.scenario: A developer is deciding which routinely-delegated skills are worth deliberately keeping sharp, versus which are fine to let the tool fully own.
contentSections.question: Which of these pass a reasonable "worth maintaining" test — meaning: it's genuinely needed at the exact moment the tool might be unavailable, and losing it has a real cost?

items.label: Debugging a production issue without AI assistance, during exactly the kind of high-pressure moment a tool might also be down or degraded
Reasoning through a core algorithm or data-structure choice by hand, since this underlies judgment calls the tool can't fully substitute for anyway
Memorizing the exact boilerplate syntax for a common framework's most repetitive setup code
Recalling the exact flags for an obscure, rarely-used command-line tool from memory

explanation.debug_without: This is exactly the scenario where losing the skill costs the most — an outage during an incident is precisely when both the tool and the skill might be needed at once, so this clears the bar clearly.
explanation.core_algorithms: This underlies judgment the tool doesn't replace even when it's working — knowing when a hash map beats a sorted list isn't really a delegatable skill in the first place, it's closer to the reasoning a tool's suggestions still need to be checked against.
explanation.boilerplate_syntax: Exact repetitive syntax is close to pure lookup — a reference doc or a quick search covers this fine even without any AI tool, so there's little real cost to letting a tool fully own it.
explanation.obscure_cli_flags: Same logic — low-frequency, easily-looked-up information isn't worth active memory maintenance; the cost of looking it up on the rare occasion it's needed is small.

contentSections.synthesis: **A skill is worth actively maintaining if it's likely to be needed at exactly the moment a tool might be unavailable (a debugging emergency), or if it underlies judgment the tool can't substitute for even when working well (core reasoning about algorithms, architecture, tradeoffs).** Pure syntax lookup and rarely-needed trivia are fine to fully delegate — the cost of relearning them in the rare moment they're needed is small, and the time spent actively maintaining them would be wasted on the vast majority of days they're not needed at all.

contentSections.body: Actively maintain what's needed exactly when the tool might fail, or what underlies judgment the tool can't substitute for. Let it fully own pure syntax and rare-lookup trivia.

title: Choosing Tools You Can Leave
description: Evaluating an AI tool for how easily you could switch away from it if you needed to — before committing workflow, data, or habits to it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a tool choice for switching cost, not just current capability
Design a workflow that keeps switching cost low from the start

contentSections.title: The cost that's invisible until you try to leave

contentSections.body: A tool that's genuinely the best available today can still be a bad choice, if choosing it quietly makes every future choice "stay with this tool" regardless of what happens to its price, quality, or terms.

contentSections.scenario: Two developers each adopt an AI coding tool for their daily workflow. Developer A's tool stores custom prompts and project context in a proprietary format only that tool can read, and the developer has built two years of accumulated project-specific instructions inside it. Developer B's tool stores the same kind of context in plain markdown files in the project repository itself, which the tool reads but doesn't own.
contentSections.question: A year from now, if a better or cheaper alternative appears, which developer is actually free to switch?

options.label: Both equally — the decision to switch is about the new tool's quality, not the old one's storage format
