Developer B — their context lives in a format they own and any tool can read, so switching costs almost nothing beyond evaluating the new tool itself
Developer A — proprietary formats are usually more capable, so their setup is actually the stronger one

feedback.both: The new tool's quality matters, but it's not the whole decision — Developer A faces an additional cost B doesn't: two years of accumulated context, locked in a format nothing else reads, has to be rebuilt from scratch or abandoned. That's a real cost weighing against switching, independent of how good the alternative is.
feedback.b: Right. Because B's context lives in plain files the project itself owns, evaluating a new tool is just about the new tool — nothing has to be rebuilt or abandoned to try it. A's accumulated context is real value, but it's value trapped in a format that makes leaving expensive, which quietly biases every future decision toward staying regardless of merit.
feedback.a: Capability of the storage format isn't really the issue — the issue is who can read it. A proprietary format can be more powerful within its own tool and still be the worse long-term choice, because that power comes with a lock-in cost that only shows up the day someone wants to leave.

contentSections.concept: **A tool's switching cost is a real, separate property from its current capability, and it's invisible until the moment you try to leave — which is exactly when it's most expensive to discover.** Preferring open formats, plain files, and portable context from the start keeps that cost low permanently, at little or no cost to what the tool can do today.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument for avoiding capable, proprietary tools — often they're worth using specifically because they're better today. It's an argument for noticing, at adoption time, which parts of the workflow are genuinely tool-specific (fine to lose if you switch) and which are actually general project knowledge that happens to be typed into a tool (worth keeping portable). Prompts and instructions that describe the project — its conventions, its domain rules, its known gotchas — are almost always the second kind, and belong in the repository, in a format any future tool can read, regardless of which specific tool is generating from them today.

Switching cost is invisible until you try to leave. Keep genuinely portable knowledge — project conventions, domain rules — in open formats the project owns, regardless of which tool reads them today.

contentSections.title: A quick evaluation before adopting anything new

contentSections.body: Before committing real workflow to a new tool, a short set of questions catches most of the lock-in risk in advance.

contentSections.intro: You're evaluating a new AI coding tool that's noticeably better than your current one on a benchmark that matters to your work. Build the switching-cost evaluation before adopting it.

fields.prompt: What should you check about how the tool stores your project context and custom instructions?
options: Nothing — storage format doesn't matter if the tool is good enough
Whether it's stored in an open, portable format you control, or a proprietary one only the tool can read
Only whether it has an export button, regardless of the export format
fields.correctValue: Whether it's stored in an open, portable format you control, or a proprietary one only the tool can read
fields.feedback: This is the concept-flow exercise's core distinction — an export button that dumps into a proprietary format the tool itself invented doesn't actually solve the lock-in problem; a genuinely open, standard format does.

fields.prompt: What should you check about pricing before committing daily workflow to it?
options: Only today's price
Today's price, and whether anything (an annual contract, a hard-to-cancel plan) locks that price in past a point you could walk away easily
Whether it's the cheapest option available right now
fields.correctValue: Today's price, and whether anything (an annual contract, a hard-to-cancel plan) locks that price in past a point you could walk away easily
fields.feedback: A great price today with a hard-to-exit annual commitment is a different risk profile than the same price month-to-month — the commitment itself is a switching cost, independent of whether the price ever actually changes.

fields.prompt: What should you check about how deeply the tool integrates into daily workflow?
options: How impressive the integration feels
Whether the integration is additive (works alongside standard tools) or replaces a standard workflow entirely with something tool-specific
Whether it has the most keyboard shortcuts
fields.correctValue: Whether the integration is additive (works alongside standard tools) or replaces a standard workflow entirely with something tool-specific
fields.feedback: A tool that layers onto a standard git/editor workflow can be dropped with the underlying workflow still intact. A tool that replaces the standard workflow with something proprietary makes leaving mean relearning how to work, not just switching a subscription.

contentSections.synthesis: **Three checks before adopting: is context stored in a format you own, is pricing genuinely flexible or quietly locked in, and does the workflow stay usable if the tool is removed.** None of this is a reason to avoid a genuinely better tool — it's what keeps "genuinely better" the only reason you're using it, rather than "too expensive to leave" becoming a second, unexamined reason alongside it.

contentSections.body: Three checks before adopting a new tool: portable context storage, genuinely flexible pricing, and a workflow that survives the tool being removed.

contentSections.title: Keep a task set, rerun it on every new model

contentSections.body:
Choosing tools you can leave is easier if you can answer one question quickly: is the new option actually better for my work? Most people answer it by feel, or by reading someone else's benchmark that has nothing to do with their tasks.

The cheap alternative is a small kept task set. Save five tasks you really do, each with the standard of good you wrote for it: the example, the yes or no checks and the bad example. When a new model or tool arrives, run all five with the same briefs. Score each against the checks. Write down time and cost beside the quality.

Then look at one table, not five impressions. Switch only the tasks where the new option is better for the price. Keep the set. In six months you will run it again, and you will have a real answer rather than a mood.

Keep it small. Five tasks run twice is ten runs, and that is plenty.

contentSections.problem: A new model is released and everyone says it is better. Decide, for your own weekly work, whether to switch.

steps.label: Keep five real tasks with their standard of good
steps.work: Five jobs you actually do: for example, a ticket summary, a short status report, a test for a small function, a data clean-up, a code review comment. Each has its example and its yes or no checks saved with it.
steps.why: Without a saved standard, you can only compare how the two results feel. With it, you compare results against the same checks.

steps.label: Run all five on both, with identical briefs
steps.work: Same wording, same context, same example. Change only the model. Run each task twice if the task is one where results varied.
steps.why: If the briefs differ, you are comparing the briefs. Running twice tells you whether a difference is real or just variation.

steps.label: Score against the checks and record time and cost
steps.work: A table with a row per task and columns for each check passed, minutes taken and cost per run.
steps.why: Quality alone hides the price, and price alone hides the quality. You need both beside each other.

steps.label: Decide per task, not per model
steps.work: Switch the two tasks where the new model passes more checks for a similar cost. Keep the old one for the rest. Note the date and run it again at the next release.
steps.why: A new model is rarely better at everything. Deciding per task keeps the gains and the savings, and leaves you free to leave a tool without a scramble.

faded.problem: A cheaper, smaller model is released. Decide whether to use it for your weekly work.

blanks.prompt: What do you run both models on?
blanks.answer: The same kept set of real tasks, with the same briefs and the same standard of good.
accept: the kept task set with identical briefs
blanks.why: The same tasks and briefs are what make the comparison fair.

blanks.prompt: What do you record beside quality?
blanks.answer: Time and cost per run.
blanks.why: A smaller model is attractive because of price, so the price has to be in the table.

blanks.prompt: At what level do you make the switch decision?
blanks.answer: Per task, not for the model as a whole.
blanks.why: A smaller model may be good enough for the simple tasks and not for the hard ones.

contentSections.procedure: Keep a small set of real tasks with a standard of good for each. When something new arrives, run the same briefs on both, score against the checks, record time and cost, and decide task by task.

contentSections.body: Judge a new model on your own five tasks, with the same briefs and the same checks. Decide task by task.

title: Local and Offline Options, Honestly Compared
description: What a local or offline model actually gives up compared to a hosted one, stated plainly enough to decide when the tradeoff is worth it — and when the honest answer is that it isn't.

learningObjectives.text: Compare local/offline AI options to hosted ones on specific, named tradeoffs
Decide when a local option is the right choice given a specific situation's constraints

contentSections.title: "Local" isn't automatically the safe choice

contentSections.body: "Just run it locally" sounds like the tool-independence answer to everything in this module — no outages, no rate limits, no ongoing subscription. It's also, honestly, usually a smaller, less capable model doing a harder job on your own hardware, and pretending that tradeoff doesn't exist helps nobody.

contentSections.scenario: A developer is comparing a locally-run open-weight coding model to their usual hosted tool, trying to be honest about what actually changes.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real, honest tradeoffs of going local — not exaggerated in either direction?

items.label: The local model is very likely to be noticeably less capable on complex, multi-step reasoning tasks than the best hosted models
It genuinely removes dependency on a provider's uptime, rate limits, and pricing changes for that specific workload
Code and data never leave the machine, which can resolve real confidentiality or data-residency concerns from earlier in this phase
It's generally easier to set up and maintain than a hosted subscription
It has no real cost once set up, since there's no subscription

explanation.capability_gap: This is real and worth saying plainly rather than downplaying — the best hosted models are, as of any given moment, generally ahead of what's practical to run locally on typical hardware, especially for harder reasoning tasks. Pretending otherwise sets up a bad surprise later.
explanation.no_dependency: This is the genuine upside this module has been building toward — for the specific workload running locally, outages and rate limits from a provider simply don't apply anymore.
explanation.data_control: This directly answers the confidentiality and NDA concerns from the accountability module — a local model is one real way to resolve "can this be pasted into a tool" for genuinely sensitive code, since nothing leaves the machine.
explanation.always_easier: Not honest — setup, hardware requirements, and keeping a local model updated is real, often nontrivial work, especially for anyone without a systems background. This is a cost, not a convenience.
explanation.always_free: Also not honest — hardware costs money (and depreciates), electricity costs money, and the developer's own setup and maintenance time costs money in the same way lesson one insisted friction time counts.

contentSections.synthesis: **A local model trades some capability for real independence from a provider's uptime, limits, and pricing, and for genuine data control — and it costs real setup time, hardware, and maintenance, not nothing.** The honest version of "should I go local" weighs a specific capability gap against a specific independence gain for a specific workload, not a general verdict that local is either always worse or always the safe answer.

contentSections.body: Local trades some capability for real independence and data control, and costs real setup and maintenance — not a free or automatically safer default.

contentSections.title: When the tradeoff is actually worth it

contentSections.body: The honest comparison from the first pod turns into a decision only when it's applied to one specific, real situation instead of debated in the abstract.

contentSections.title: The confidential codebase and the capability gap
contentSections.opening: You're contracted on a project with strict data-residency and confidentiality requirements — the kind flagged in the accountability module's four pre-engagement checks — where no general-purpose hosted AI tool is clearly covered by the client's agreement. The work involves fairly standard, well-understood application code, not cutting-edge algorithmic work.

decide.situation: You're deciding how to handle AI assistance on this specific project.
decide.question: What's the right call?

choices.label: Use your usual hosted tool anyway, reasoning the capability gap with local models isn't worth the switch
choices.consequence: This repeats exactly the confidentiality risk the accountability module warned about — an uncovered third party receiving client data, regardless of how good the tool is.

choices.label: Avoid AI assistance entirely on this project to be safe, accepting whatever productivity cost that carries
choices.consequence: This avoids the confidentiality risk completely but gives up a real, available option without checking whether it actually solves the problem.

choices.label: Evaluate a local model specifically for this project's kind of work, weighing the real capability gap against the real confidentiality win

eval.situation: You test a capable local model against a sample of the actual, fairly standard application code this project involves — CRUD endpoints, form validation, typical business logic.
eval.question: The local model performs close to as well as your hosted tool on this specific, standard kind of work — the capability gap that matters most on harder algorithmic tasks barely shows up here. What do you conclude?

choices.label: Adopt the local model for this project specifically, since the capability gap that would matter is small for this particular kind of work and the confidentiality win is real and needed
Avoid AI assistance anyway, since the local option still isn't quite as good as the hosted one in the abstract

risked.summary: The productivity stayed high, but the actual confidentiality risk from earlier in the phase went unaddressed — the capability comparison happened, but the constraint that mattered most for this project didn't get weighed at all.
risked.lesson: This is what happens when "is the local model good enough" gets asked without first asking whether the situation actually requires the independence it buys — for a project with a real, binding confidentiality constraint, that constraint should have been the first filter, not an afterthought weighed against convenience.

overcautious.summary: The confidentiality risk is fully avoided, but so is a real, close-enough-for-this-work option that would have solved the actual problem without the productivity cost.
overcautious.lesson: Caution without evaluation isn't actually the safe choice, it's just a different way of not doing the analysis — the case-sim's eval step showed the gap that mattered was small for this specific, standard kind of work, information that only came from actually testing it, not from assuming local always means a worse outcome.

resolved.summary: A real constraint gets a real fix, matched specifically to the kind of work this project involves rather than to a general opinion about local models.
resolved.lesson: The right call came from testing the actual tradeoff against the actual work, not from a blanket rule in either direction — a local model that's clearly behind on hard algorithmic work can still be the right, fully sufficient choice for typical application code, and the only way to know is to check, for this project, against this kind of task.

contentSections.body: Test the actual tradeoff against the actual work in front of you. A local model's capability gap matters most on hard tasks and can be nearly invisible on standard ones — the only way to know is to check, not assume.

title: Practice — Cost and De-risk Seven Tool-Dependent Workflows
description: Seven drills across real cost, outage planning, skill maintenance, and tool lock-in. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's cost, contingency and independence standards to unfamiliar situations
Evaluate a tool-dependent workflow for its real risk

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven situations, each needing a cost calculation, a contingency decision, or a lock-in evaluation. Do them in one sitting or three.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint.

title: Lab — Deliver a Change With Your Primary Tool Unavailable
description: Complete a real, bounded change while deliberately not using your primary AI tool, and produce an honest account of what slowed down and by how much.

learningObjectives.text: Complete real work without the primary AI tool
Quantify the actual cost of tool unavailability on a real task

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every other exercise in this module has reasoned about tool unavailability. This lab makes it real: one bounded task, primary tool genuinely off, tracked honestly.

contentSections.title: A change, without your primary tool
contentSections.brief: Pick one small, real, bounded piece of work — similar in size to the estimating module's lab task. Complete it with your primary AI coding tool deliberately turned off or unused throughout, using only what lesson three called your actively-maintained skills, reference docs, and — if you choose, per lesson five — a local model as the one exception.
contentSections.deliverable: The finished change, plus a written note comparing this task's actual time to your normal AI-assisted estimate for the same kind of work, naming specifically what slowed down and why.

stages.title: Pick the task and set the ground rule
stages.instructions: Choose a task you could estimate confidently using the estimating module's procedure if your usual tool were available. Decide explicitly whether a local model is in scope as an exception, per lesson five, or whether this is fully manual.
stages.checkpoint: The task is chosen and the ground rule (fully manual, or local-model-assisted) is stated before starting.

stages.title: Estimate it as if the tool were available
stages.instructions: Write a quick estimate for this task using the review-first procedure from the estimating module, as a baseline for comparison later.
stages.checkpoint: A baseline estimate exists, written before the work starts.

stages.title: Do the work without the primary tool
stages.instructions: Complete the task. Notice, in real time, where you reach for a skill from lesson three's maintained list, where you're slower than usual, and where a workaround (documentation, a local model, manual reasoning) stands in for what the tool would normally do.
stages.checkpoint: The task is genuinely finished without the primary tool.

stages.title: Log what actually slowed things down
stages.instructions: List the specific points where the absence of the tool cost time, and roughly how much — not a vague "it was slower," but named moments (e.g. "spent 12 minutes writing the regex by hand that the tool usually generates instantly").
stages.checkpoint: At least two or three specific, timed slowdowns are named.

stages.title: Write the comparison note
stages.instructions: Compare actual time to the baseline estimate. State honestly whether the gap was mostly capability (things you genuinely couldn't do as well) or mostly friction (things that just took longer), per this module's distinctions.
stages.checkpoint: The note distinguishes capability cost from friction cost, not just a single "it took longer" statement.

rubric.criterion: The task is genuinely completed without the primary tool

title: Checkpoint — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
description: Ten questions, 40% this module, 40% the previous module (Working With a Team, and Without One), 20% from earlier in the phase.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and reconnect them to the phase's earlier modules

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four from Working With a Team, and Without One, two from earlier in the phase.

questions.from: This module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: What does the real monthly cost of AI tool use include, beyond the headline subscription price?

options.label: Every tool actually used at real usage rates, plus time lost to friction like rate limits and outages
Nothing — the subscription price is the real cost
Only usage-based API charges, not time

questions.explanation: The headline price is often less than half the real total once every actually-used tool and honestly-timed friction are counted.

questions.from: This module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: What are the three named failure modes worth planning a fallback for?

options.label: Full outage, rate limit, and degraded response — each with a different appropriate fallback
Only full outages matter; the others are rare enough to ignore
Slow internet, browser crashes, and typos

questions.explanation: Each of the three has a genuinely different signature and right response — waiting out a rate limit is often fine, waiting out a full outage against a fixed deadline usually isn't.

questions.from: This module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: Which skills does the module say are worth actively maintaining despite heavy tool reliance?

options.label: Skills needed at exactly the moment the tool might fail, and skills underlying judgment the tool can't substitute for
Every skill the tool currently handles, without exception
Only skills related to security

questions.explanation: Debugging during an outage and core algorithmic/architectural judgment both clear the bar; pure boilerplate syntax and rare lookup trivia don't need active maintenance.

questions.from: This module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: What makes a tool's context storage a switching-cost risk?

options.label: A proprietary format that only that tool can read locks in accumulated value and makes leaving expensive
Any format is equally portable as long as there's an export button
Storage format has no effect on switching cost

questions.explanation: An export into another proprietary format doesn't solve lock-in — genuinely open, standard formats the project itself owns are what keep switching cost low.

questions.from: Previous module — Working With a Team, and Without One
questions.prompt: What makes an async update actually useful, rather than just brief?

options.label: It answers the questions a reader far away in time would otherwise have to ask and wait on
It's as short as possible
It uses formal, professional language

questions.explanation: A short update missing what was tested is just as blocking as a long one — the test is whether a distant reader can act on it alone.

questions.from: Previous module — Working With a Team, and Without One

options.label: Fix the specific bug now, give the general concern a real venue elsewhere
Dismiss the general concern to stay on topic
Resolve the general debate before touching the bug

questions.from: Previous module — Working With a Team, and Without One

options.label: Re-reading your own recent reasoning tends to confirm it rather than challenge it
People reviewing their own code don't try hard enough
Self-review only fails on AI-generated code

Decline with no further response

The whole job, roughly proportionally

The AI tool

title: The Brief, and What It Doesn't Say
description: Reading a real brief for what it's actually asking versus what it assumes without saying — the first, easy-to-rush step of the capstone.

learningObjectives.text: Extract the real requirements and unstated assumptions from a realistic brief
Identify what a brief is silent on that will still need a decision

contentSections.title: A brief is a compressed version of a real need

contentSections.body: "Add the ability to export a customer's order history to a spreadsheet" is eleven words. It compresses a real business need, a set of unstated assumptions about format and scope, and at least three decisions nobody's made yet — and treating it as a complete spec is how a finished feature misses the actual point.

contentSections.scenario: A real-shaped capstone brief: "Customers keep emailing support asking for their order history so they can reconcile it with their own accounting. Can we add an export feature to the account page?" Two developers read this. One starts building a CSV export button immediately. The other first asks: which fields does accounting reconciliation actually need, is CSV the right format for whatever accounting tool customers likely use, does this need to cover refunds and partial orders as their own line items, and is there a date-range limit worth imposing for very old accounts.
contentSections.question: What's the real difference between these two developers' starting points?

options.label: The first developer is faster, which matters more than the questions the second one is asking
The first developer is building to the literal eleven words; the second is building to the actual stated need — reconciling with accounting — which the eleven words only gestured at
There's no real difference; both will end up building the same thing

feedback.faster: Starting immediately isn't actually faster once the literal-reading version has to be reworked after a customer explains, post-launch, that the export doesn't have the fields their accounting software needs — which is a predictable outcome of skipping the questions, not bad luck.
feedback.real_need: Right, and this is the whole point of the brief-reading step: the literal request ("an export feature") is a stand-in for the real need (accounting reconciliation), stated by the customers themselves in the brief. Building the literal version without checking against the real need risks shipping something that technically satisfies the sentence and doesn't solve the actual problem.
feedback.same: They're likely to diverge specifically on the things the second developer asked about — field selection, format, refund handling, date range — none of which the eleven-word brief settled, and each of which a reasonable literal reading could get wrong relative to what accounting reconciliation actually needs.

contentSections.concept: **A brief states a request; it rarely states the need behind the request in enough detail to build correctly, and the gap between them is exactly where a technically-complete feature misses the point.** Reading a brief well means treating the literal words as a pointer to the real need, not as the finished spec — and the real need is usually recoverable by asking what the requester is actually trying to accomplish, as it was here: reconciling with accounting software.

contentSections.body: This isn't a new skill introduced for the capstone — it's the estimating module's unknown-naming skill and the scoping module's evidence-stack pattern, applied at the very start of a project instead of mid-estimate. The capstone doesn't teach anything new here; it asks you to actually do it, on one real piece of work, instead of on an exercise.
A brief states a request; it rarely states the need. Read for the need — usually recoverable by asking what the requester is actually trying to accomplish.

contentSections.title: What the brief is silent on

contentSections.body: Beyond the stated need, every real brief is silent on things that will still require a decision — and silence isn't the same as "anything goes."

contentSections.scenario: Reading the order-history-export brief again, a developer is listing what it's genuinely silent on.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real silences worth resolving before or during the build, not just implementation details to pick freely?

items.label: Whether this export includes any data a customer shouldn't see about their own account (e.g. internal notes, cost basis, fraud flags)
Whether an account with ten years and thousands of orders should export everything at once or needs pagination/date limits
What exact text the export button should say
How to handle orders in multiple currencies if the account has them, for a spreadsheet reconciliation use case specifically

explanation.who_can_export: This is a real, silent risk: any export feature is a natural place to accidentally expose internal-only fields that happen to live in the same order record — worth an explicit check, not an assumption that the existing display logic already handles it.
explanation.volume: A brief that doesn't mention volume doesn't mean volume isn't a real constraint — a large account exporting thousands of rows at once could be a genuine performance or usability problem worth deciding on deliberately.
explanation.button_label: This is exactly the kind of detail any reasonable choice satisfies — not a silence that needs resolving before building, just an implementation detail.
explanation.currency: Given the explicit accounting-reconciliation need, multi-currency handling isn't a minor detail — getting it wrong could make the export actively unusable for the exact purpose it was requested for.

contentSections.synthesis: **A brief's silence on data exposure, scale, and anything tied directly to the stated real need is a silence worth resolving deliberately — a brief's silence on cosmetic implementation choices is not.** The same distinction the estimating module drew between unknowns worth naming and coding details to just build applies here, at the very start of the capstone.

contentSections.body: A brief's silence on data exposure, scale, or anything tied to the real stated need is worth resolving deliberately. Silence on cosmetic details isn't.

title: Planning the Change Against Your Own Take-Over Rule
description: Deciding, before writing any code, which parts of the capstone change get AI-generated and which get written by hand — using the same review-time and ownership reasoning from earlier in the phase.

learningObjectives.text: Plan a real change's AI-assistance boundaries before starting
Apply the module's earlier cost and ownership reasoning to a real planning decision

contentSections.title: Deciding the boundary before you're mid-task

contentSections.body: The moment to decide which parts of a change deserve heavy manual reasoning and which parts are safe to generate quickly isn't while deep in the code, tempted by however plausible the next suggestion looks. It's now, on paper, before any of it feels urgent.

contentSections.problem: Planning the order-history-export capstone change (from lesson one, real need: accounting reconciliation). It touches: the export button and UI, the query that gathers order data, the CSV formatting logic, the currency-conversion handling for multi-currency accounts, and a rate limit on how often one account can trigger a large export. Decide, before writing anything, which parts get generated freely and which get extra manual scrutiny.

steps.label: Apply the estimating module's familiarity-and-consequence test to each part
steps.work: UI button: familiar, low consequence — generate freely. Query logic: familiar pattern, moderate consequence (wrong data is bad but visible/checkable) — generate, review carefully. CSV formatting: familiar, low-moderate consequence — generate, spot-check. Currency conversion: less familiar territory, high consequence (wrong numbers silently break the stated reconciliation need) — write core logic by hand, verify heavily. Rate limiting: moderate familiarity, moderate consequence (get it wrong and it either blocks legitimate use or fails to protect the system) — generate, review against known rate-limit pitfalls.
steps.why: This is the exact test from the estimating module's lesson two, applied here at planning time instead of after code already exists — deciding the scrutiny level in advance means the currency-conversion code gets the manual attention it needs from the start, not as an afterthought once a bug is found.

steps.label: Name the explicit take-over rule
steps.work: Write a one-sentence rule for this specific change: "Anything that computes a number that ends up in the exported spreadsheet gets manually written and unit-tested by hand; everything else (UI, query shape, formatting) can be AI-generated and reviewed normally."
steps.why: A specific, written rule — not a vague "be careful with the money parts" — is checkable while building: for any given line, does it compute a number in the export, yes or no. That's a rule you can actually apply consistently under time pressure.

steps.label: Connect the rule to the ownership standard
steps.work: Recall the accountability module's ownership bar: being able to explain the code in a case not shown, and having weighed the risk if it's wrong. The take-over rule is really just naming, in advance, where that bar needs to be met by writing it yourself rather than by reviewing someone (something) else's draft.
steps.why: This ties the capstone's planning step directly back to the phase's foundational standard — the take-over rule isn't a new concept, it's the ownership bar applied prospectively, at the one point (before starting) where it's cheapest to apply.

steps.label: Write it into the plan, not just decide it privately
steps.work: Add the take-over rule as a visible line in the change's planning notes, so it's checkable later — during the review lesson and the defence lesson — whether it was actually followed.
steps.why: A private decision is easy to quietly abandon under deadline pressure. A written one is checkable — including by the developer themselves, later, during the self-review stage of the lab.

faded.problem: A second capstone-shaped example: a change that adds an automated email reminder for customers with abandoned carts, including the trigger logic (when to send), the email content generation, and an unsubscribe/suppression check.

blanks.prompt: Which part is most clearly high-consequence and worth a manual take-over, given what an email system getting it wrong actually does?
blanks.answer: the unsubscribe/suppression check
blanks.why: Getting suppression wrong means emailing someone who explicitly opted out — a real trust and, in many jurisdictions, compliance problem, unlike a subtly-off email subject line.

blanks.prompt: Write a one-sentence take-over rule for this change, in the style of the worked example's rule.
blanks.answer: anything that determines whether or to whom an email actually gets sent is written and tested by hand; the email content and trigger-timing logic can be generated and reviewed normally
accept: the send/suppress decision logic is hand-written; content generation is AI-assisted
blanks.why: This mirrors the worked example's rule shape: a specific, checkable line (does this code decide whether the email sends) rather than a vague instruction to be careful with the important parts.

blanks.prompt: Where should this rule be written down, per step 4?
blanks.answer: in the change's planning notes, visibly, not just decided privately
accept: documented, not just decided in your head
blanks.why: The same reasoning applies here as in the worked example — a rule that isn't written down is easy to quietly abandon once the deadline gets close.

contentSections.procedure: **Apply the familiarity-and-consequence test to every part of the planned change, write a specific, checkable take-over rule naming exactly which code gets hand-written, tie it explicitly to the ownership standard, and put it in writing before starting.** This is where the capstone's planning stage earns its name — it's a real decision made in advance, not a description of what happened to occur while building.

contentSections.body: Write a specific, checkable take-over rule before starting — which code gets hand-written because it computes something high-consequence — not a vague intention to be careful.

contentSections.title: Planning the stages

contentSections.body: The scoping module's staging lesson applies here too — a capstone change is exactly the kind of work that benefits from being broken into checkable stages rather than one long, unresumable block.

contentSections.question: For the order-history-export change (query/data-shaping, currency handling, CSV formatting/export, rate limit, UI polish), roughly how many independently checkable stages would a well-staged plan use — fewer than 3, exactly 5, or more than 8?
contentSections.answer: Around 5 — one per natural checkable unit (query, currency logic, CSV/export, rate limit, UI/PR write-up), matching the 3–5 range this track's labs have used throughout.
contentSections.hint: Too few stages loses the resumability benefit; too many turns staging into busywork rather than real checkpoints.

contentSections.body:
Before building, sketch the change as 3–5 stages, the way this track's labs have been staged throughout — each one independently checkable, each a real stopping point. For the order-history-export example: (1) the query and data-shaping logic, checkable by running it against a real account and eyeballing the output; (2) the currency-handling logic specifically, checkable against a small set of known-correct hand-calculated examples; (3) the CSV formatting and export endpoint, checkable by actually opening the file in a spreadsheet tool; (4) the rate limit, checkable by triggering it deliberately; (5) UI polish and the PR write-up.

This isn't extra process for its own sake — it's what makes the review and defence lessons that follow possible to do well. A defence of "why this, not that" is much easier to write about five distinct, already-checked stages than about one large diff where the reasoning for each part has blurred together by the time it's finished.
Stage the capstone change into 3–5 independently checkable pieces before starting — it's what makes the review and defence stages that follow actually possible to do well.

title: Reviewing Your Own Work as a Stranger Would
description: Applying the module's earlier self-review procedure at full strength to a real, finished piece of capstone work — not a drill, the actual change.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the failure-mode-hunting self-review procedure to a real, complete change
Distinguish a genuine review from a confirming re-read on real work

contentSections.title: The review that actually counts

contentSections.body: Every self-review exercise in this phase so far has been practice. This one is the change that's actually going to ship — which is exactly the moment the confirmation bias from the teamwork module's lesson five is strongest, because there's real momentum and real desire for it to just be done.

contentSections.scenario: A developer finishing the capstone change feels a strong pull to call the self-review "done" quickly — the change works, the happy path is verified, it's been a long stretch of focused work, and there's real satisfaction in seeing it functional. They notice the pull and pause before deciding how to review.
contentSections.question: What does the teamwork module's mechanism predict is the actual risk in this exact moment, specifically?

options.label: The risk is generic tiredness making them careless

The satisfaction of having just finished something that works is itself a strong version of the confirming-re-read bias — the review is happening at the exact moment motivation to find problems is lowest
There's no elevated risk here specifically — every review carries the same baseline risk

feedback.tired: Tiredness is a real, separate risk, but it's not what's specific to this moment — the described pull is toward wanting it to be done, which is a motivated version of the confirmation problem, not simple fatigue.
feedback.motivated_reasoning: This is the sharpest version of the mechanism from earlier in this phase: it's not just that reviewing your own recent reasoning tends to confirm it — here there's an added, real desire for the review to come back clean, because the work is finished and it feels good. That's exactly the condition the failure-mode-hunting frame ("what would make this wrong") was designed to counteract, and it matters most precisely when the pull to skip it is strongest.
feedback.no_risk: The risk here is actually higher than a routine mid-project review, not equal to baseline — genuine completion satisfaction is a stronger pull toward a confirming read than an ordinary checkpoint moment, which is exactly why this is where the procedure needs to be followed most rigorously, not relaxed.

contentSections.mechanism: **The moment a change feels finished and satisfying is the moment self-review is structurally weakest, not neutral — motivation to find problems is lowest exactly when the desire to be done is highest.** This is the teamwork module's confirmation mechanism at its strongest, and it's exactly why the capstone asks for the full procedure here rather than a shortcut earned by how much work already went in.

contentSections.body: Completion satisfaction is a stronger pull toward a confirming read than an ordinary review moment — which is exactly when the full self-review procedure matters most, not least.

contentSections.title: Running the procedure at full strength

contentSections.body: The procedure itself doesn't change for the capstone. What changes is running every piece of it, deliberately, instead of letting completion momentum shortcut any of it.

contentSections.intro: Apply the teamwork module's self-review procedure to the finished capstone change, at full strength.

fields.prompt: Given the elevated motivated-reasoning risk just diagnosed, how should the gap before reviewing be handled here specifically?
options: Skip it — the change has already taken a long time, a gap just delays shipping further
Take it seriously, even more than usual — step away for a real break, not a token few minutes, given how strong the completion pull is
A gap isn't relevant to self-review at all
fields.correctValue: Take it seriously, even more than usual — step away for a real break, not a token few minutes, given how strong the completion pull is
fields.feedback: Since the diagnose-mechanism exercise found the confirming pull is stronger here than in a routine review, the gap that counteracts it needs to be taken at least as seriously, not shortened because the project already ran long.

fields.prompt: What should the review question be, applied to the whole finished change?
options: "Does this work?" — since it clearly runs and produces the right output on the cases tried
"What would make this wrong, specifically in the parts I generated versus the parts I hand-wrote under the take-over rule?"
"Is this good enough to stop working on?"
fields.correctValue: "What would make this wrong, specifically in the parts I generated versus the parts I hand-wrote under the take-over rule?"
fields.feedback: This connects the failure-hunting frame directly to lesson two's take-over rule — the review should specifically re-check that the high-consequence, hand-written parts actually got the scrutiny the plan called for, not just confirm the change runs.

fields.prompt: What should the checklist include, specific to this capstone change (using the order-history-export example)?
options: A generic checklist copied from an unrelated project
The specific unknowns and silences named back in lesson one, plus the take-over rule's named high-consequence parts, checked explicitly against the finished code
No checklist — the reviewer's judgment in the moment is enough
fields.correctValue: The specific unknowns and silences named back in lesson one, plus the take-over rule's named high-consequence parts, checked explicitly against the finished code
fields.feedback: This is what makes the review specific rather than generic — checking the finished code against the actual unknowns named at the start (data exposure, multi-currency handling, scale) is far more likely to catch a real gap than a checklist borrowed from somewhere else.

fields.prompt: What should the review produce, given this feeds directly into the defence lesson that follows?
options: Nothing written — just a private decision to ship or not
A written note connecting each of lesson one's named unknowns and lesson two's take-over rule to what was actually found in review — the raw material for the defence
A one-word verdict: pass or fail
fields.correctValue: A written note connecting each of lesson one's named unknowns and lesson two's take-over rule to what was actually found in review — the raw material for the defence
fields.feedback: This is deliberately not optional here — the next lesson's defence has to explain why specific decisions were made, and the honest, in-the-moment review notes are what make that defence real instead of a reconstruction written after the fact to sound good.

contentSections.synthesis: **The procedure doesn't change for the capstone — what changes is refusing the shortcut completion satisfaction offers, and connecting every step explicitly back to what was actually planned in lessons one and two, so the resulting notes are real material for the defence, not a retrofit.**

contentSections.body: The self-review procedure doesn't change for the capstone — what has to change is refusing the shortcut completion satisfaction offers, and writing the review as real material for the defence that follows.

title: Writing the Defence: Why This, Not That
description: Writing a defence of the capstone change's real decisions — the ones with a genuine alternative someone could reasonably have picked instead.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which decisions in a finished change actually need defending
Write a defence that would satisfy a skeptical, informed reviewer

contentSections.title: Not every decision needs defending

contentSections.body: A defence that tries to justify every single choice in a change — including the ones with no real alternative — reads as padding and buries the two or three decisions that actually mattered under a pile of ones that didn't.

contentSections.scenario: Reviewing the finished order-history-export change for what actually needs defending: (1) the choice to use CSV rather than a different spreadsheet format, (2) the choice of variable names in the query function, (3) the choice to hand-write the currency-conversion logic rather than generate it, per the take-over rule, (4) the choice not to support a custom date range in this first version.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely need a written defence — a real alternative existed and a reasonable person might ask why it wasn't chosen?

options.label: All four, equally, since a thorough defence covers everything
1, 3, and 4 — each has a real, reasonable alternative someone could point to; 2 doesn't
Only 3, since it's the only one connected to the take-over rule

feedback.all: Treating variable naming as needing the same defence as a format choice or a scope-limiting decision dilutes the document — a reader skimming a defence that spends equal weight on trivial and consequential choices learns to skim past all of it, including the parts that matter.
feedback.three: Right. CSV-versus-another-format, hand-writing-versus-generating the currency logic, and cutting date-range support from v1 are all decisions with a real, articulable alternative a reasonable reviewer might independently favor — that's exactly what makes them worth defending. Variable naming has no comparably real alternative anyone would seriously propose instead.
feedback.only3: The take-over rule decision does need defending, but it's not alone — the format choice and the scope-cutting decision are equally real "why this, not that" moments, just from different lessons in this module rather than lesson two specifically.

contentSections.concept: **A decision needs defending when a reasonable, informed person could have made a different choice and might ask why you didn't.** Format choices, scope cuts, and take-over-rule calls all clear that bar. Implementation details with no real alternative — most naming, most formatting — don't, and defending them anyway just buries the decisions that do.

contentSections.body: Defend a decision only if a reasonable, informed person could have chosen differently and might ask why you didn't. Everything else is padding.

contentSections.title: Writing a defence that would actually survive a skeptical question

contentSections.body: A defence that just restates the decision ("I chose CSV because it's a common format") isn't a defence — it's a description. The real version says what was weighed and why it came out the way it did.

contentSections.problem: Write the defence for the decision to cut custom date-range support from the first version of the order-history-export feature.

steps.label: State the decision plainly
steps.work: "V1 exports full order history with no custom date-range filter."
steps.why: A defence that buries the actual decision in hedging wastes the reader's time before it even gets to the reasoning.

steps.label: Name the real alternative
steps.work: "The alternative was building a date-range picker in this same release, which was technically straightforward given the existing query structure."
steps.why: Naming the road not taken, honestly, is what separates a real defence from a justification written to sound good after the fact — it shows the alternative was actually considered, not invented as a strawman.

steps.label: State the actual reasoning, including the tradeoff
steps.work: "Cut for this release because the stated need — reconciling with accounting software — is satisfied by a full export in every case observed in support tickets; no request mentioned wanting a partial range. Adding it now would have meant less review time on the currency-conversion logic, which the take-over rule flagged as the actually high-consequence part of this change."
steps.why: This is the part a description skips and a real defence includes: what got traded for what, and why that trade was the right one given what actually mattered most in this specific change — connecting back to lesson two's take-over rule explicitly.

steps.label: Say what would change the decision
steps.work: "If a support ticket specifically requests date-range filtering, that's a fast, well-scoped follow-up — the query already supports it structurally, it's the UI and validation that were cut."
steps.why: This shows the decision was made with real information about how it could be revisited, not as a door quietly closed — which is what actually reassures a skeptical reviewer that scope was cut deliberately, not carelessly.

faded.problem: Now defend the decision to hand-write the currency-conversion logic rather than generate it, per the take-over rule from lesson two.

blanks.prompt: State the decision plainly, in one sentence.
blanks.answer: the currency-conversion logic was written by hand rather than AI-generated
accept: currency conversion was hand-written, not generated
blanks.why: Same principle as the worked example — state it before defending it.

blanks.prompt: Name the real alternative that was available.
blanks.answer: generating it with the AI tool, the same way the query and CSV formatting logic were, and reviewing it afterward
accept: generating it like the rest of the change and reviewing carefully
blanks.why: The real alternative here is exactly what happened with the rest of the change — this makes the contrast, and the reason for it, concrete rather than abstract.

blanks.prompt: State the actual reasoning in one sentence, referencing the take-over rule.
blanks.answer: the take-over rule flagged anything computing a number in the export as high-consequence, since a silent currency error would break the stated reconciliation need without being visibly wrong
accept: it's high-consequence per the take-over rule — wrong numbers would silently break the reconciliation use case
blanks.why: This is the actual defence, not a restatement — it explains why this specific piece crossed the threshold the take-over rule set, tying back to lesson two directly.

contentSections.procedure: **State the decision plainly, name the real alternative honestly, give the actual reasoning including what was traded for what, and say what would change the decision later.** A defence built this way is checkable and specific — a reader can disagree with the reasoning, but they can't say it wasn't given.

contentSections.body: A real defence states the decision, names the honest alternative, gives the actual reasoning and tradeoff, and says what would revisit it — not just a restated choice dressed up as a justification.

title: What You'd Do Differently With Another Week
description: Writing an honest, specific account of the corners genuinely cut under real constraints — the closing move that makes a defence trustworthy rather than a performance of confidence.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a genuine account of cut corners from false modesty or a real problem being minimized
Write a specific, honest account of what a real time constraint actually cost the work

contentSections.title: The question that isn't "what would you improve"

contentSections.body: "What would you improve" invites a vague, safe answer — more tests, cleaner code, the kind of thing that's true of literally every piece of software ever shipped and says nothing specific. "What would you do differently with another week" is a sharper question, and it has a real, specific answer if the work was actually done under a real constraint.

contentSections.code: Capstone closing note: "With more time I would have written more tests and cleaned up the code further. Overall I'm happy with how this turned out."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this closing note, given the whole module's standard for honest accounting?

options.label: It's too short
"More tests" and "cleaner code" are generic enough to be true of nearly any shipped feature — they don't name a specific, real corner that was actually cut on this change
It shouldn't end on a positive note

feedback.short: Length isn't the issue — a short, specific account ("I didn't verify the currency-conversion logic against a real multi-currency account, only synthetic test data") would be more useful than a long, generic one.
feedback.generic: Right — this is the same test the disclosure module applied to PR descriptions: would removing this sentence cost a reader real information? "More tests" fails that test the same way a boilerplate AI-use caution note did, because it's true of nearly every piece of software regardless of what actually happened on this project specifically.
feedback.positive: Ending on genuine confidence in the work is fine and often accurate — the flaw isn't the tone, it's that the substance underneath the tone doesn't name anything real about this specific change's actual constraints.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A genuine version names something specific and true about this particular change under its actual constraints: "With another week, the currency-conversion logic would get tested against real historical multi-currency orders instead of the five synthetic cases I hand-built — synthetic cases are a reasonable stand-in under this timeline, but they're not the same confidence level as real data, and that's the honest gap in this specific change." That's checkable, specific to what actually happened, and consistent with the take-over rule's own reasoning about where the real risk in this change lives.

contentSections.body: A generic "more tests, cleaner code" answer says nothing specific about this change. Name the real, specific corner that was actually cut under the actual constraint.

contentSections.title: Closing the loop on the whole capstone

contentSections.body: This closing note isn't separate from everything else in the capstone — it's the place where lesson one's named unknowns, lesson two's take-over rule, and lesson three's review findings all get to point at whatever's still actually uncertain, honestly, one more time.

contentSections.question: A strong closing note should trace back to one of three sources from earlier in the capstone. Before reading on, guess: what are they likely to be, given lessons one through three?
contentSections.answer: An unknown from lesson one resolved by assumption rather than confirmation, a take-over-rule boundary from lesson two that was drawn slightly wrong in hindsight, or a review finding from lesson three that got mitigated rather than fully resolved.
contentSections.hint: Think about what each of the first three lessons produced that could still be uncertain by the end.

contentSections.body:
A genuinely useful "what I'd do with another week" note usually traces back to one of three sources, and naming which one makes it specific instead of generic:

**An unknown from lesson one that got resolved by assumption rather than by confirmation** — "I assumed no customer needs date ranges spanning a currency redenomination event; with more time I'd confirm that with support rather than assume it from the tickets I read."

**A take-over-rule boundary that, in hindsight, was drawn slightly wrong** — "The rate-limit logic turned out to interact with the export in a way I didn't fully anticipate when I judged it medium-consequence; with more time I'd bump it to the hand-written tier."

**A review finding from lesson three that got mitigated rather than fully resolved** — "Self-review flagged that the CSV escaping hasn't been tested against a customer name containing both a comma and a quote character in the same field; I added a targeted test for the common case but didn't exhaustively fuzz it."

Each of these is specific, checkable, and honestly connects back to a real decision made earlier in the capstone — which is what makes the whole thing read as an honest account of real engineering under real constraints, rather than either false modesty or an unearned victory lap.

The strongest closing note traces back to something specific from earlier in the capstone — an assumed unknown, a take-over-rule boundary, or a mitigated-not-resolved review finding — not a generic wish for more tests.

title: Lab — Ship the Capstone Change and Defend It in Writing
description: The track's capstone: take one real change from request to shipped, applying every skill from this phase, and produce a merged change with tests, a disclosure note, and a written defence of every significant decision.

learningObjectives.text: Take a real change from brief to shipped applying the full phase's skill set
Produce a complete, honest defence of a real piece of shipped work

contentSections.title: The capstone

contentSections.body: Everything in this phase has been building toward one real piece of work: a brief read for its real need, planned against an explicit take-over rule, built in checkable stages, reviewed at full strength against completion pressure, and defended honestly — corners cut and all. This lab is that change, start to finish.

contentSections.title: Ship and defend a real change
contentSections.brief: Pick one real, bounded change — from your own backlog, an open-source issue, freelance work, or a realistic simulated brief if nothing real is available right now. It should be substantial enough to have at least one genuine "why this, not that" decision in it, and small enough to actually finish. Run it through every stage of this module.
contentSections.deliverable: A shipped (or ship-ready) change, its tests, a disclosure note following the accountability module's specific-not-generic standard, and a written defence covering: the brief's real need and named unknowns, the take-over rule and why, the self-review findings, at least two genuinely defended decisions, and an honest "another week" account.

stages.title: Read the brief for its real need
stages.instructions: Write the brief as it actually arrived (or would). Following lesson one, state the real need behind it and name at least one genuine silence worth resolving before building.
stages.checkpoint: The real need is stated distinctly from the literal request, and at least one real silence is named and resolved.

stages.title: Plan the take-over rule and stages
stages.instructions: Following lesson two, apply the familiarity-and-consequence test to the change's parts, write a specific take-over rule, and sketch 3–5 checkable stages.
stages.checkpoint: A specific, checkable take-over rule is written before any code, and the stages are named.

stages.title: Build it in stages
stages.instructions: Do the work, following the planned stages and the take-over rule. Write the disclosure note as you go, per the accountability module's standard — what was generated, what was hand-written and why, what was tested.
stages.checkpoint: The change is functionally complete and the disclosure note is specific to this change, not generic.

stages.title: Run the full-strength self-review
stages.instructions: Following lesson three: take a real gap, review with the "what would make this wrong" frame, check explicitly against the unknowns and take-over rule from stages one and two, and write the review note.
stages.checkpoint: The self-review note explicitly references the unknowns and take-over rule named earlier, not just a general "looks good."

stages.title: Write the defence and the closing account
stages.instructions: Following lessons four and five: identify and defend at least two real "why this, not that" decisions (plainly stated, real alternative named, actual reasoning given), and write a specific, honest "what I'd do with another week" note tracing back to something real from the earlier stages.
stages.checkpoint: At least two decisions are defended with a named real alternative, and the closing note is specific, not generic.

rubric.criterion: The real need is distinguished from the literal brief
rubric.meets: A reader can tell what was actually being solved for, not just what was literally requested, and at least one real silence was named and resolved.

rubric.criterion: The take-over rule is specific and checkable
rubric.meets: A reader could apply the rule to a new line of code and know whether it should be hand-written or generated, based on the stated rule.

rubric.criterion: The disclosure note passes the theatre test
rubric.meets: Every sentence in it would cost a reader real information if removed — specific to this change, not a boilerplate caution.

rubric.criterion: The self-review references the actual plan, not a generic pass
rubric.meets: The review note explicitly checks the finished work against the unknowns and take-over rule named earlier in the lab.

rubric.criterion: At least two decisions are genuinely defended
rubric.meets: Each defended decision names a real alternative a reasonable person might have picked, and gives actual reasoning, not just a restated choice.

rubric.criterion: The closing account is specific and honest
rubric.meets: The "another week" note names something real and checkable, tracing back to an unknown, a take-over-rule call, or a review finding — not a generic wish for more tests.

contentSections.body: This is the whole phase in one piece of real work: a need read honestly, a boundary drawn on paper before it mattered, a review run at full strength against the pull to call it done, and a defence that would survive being asked a real question about it.

title: Checkpoint — Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
description: Ten questions, 40% this module, 40% the previous module (Cost, Limits and Tool Independence), 20% from earlier in the phase.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and reconnect them across the whole phase

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four from Cost, Limits and Tool Independence, two from earlier in the phase.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a brief's stated request and its real need?

options.label: The literal words often compress a real underlying need the brief only gestures at, which a technically-complete build can miss entirely
There's no real difference — a well-written brief states them identically
The real need is always more literal than the stated request

questions.explanation: The order-history-export example showed a literal "add an export button" reading could miss the actual accounting-reconciliation need the customers stated, if the fields, format, and multi-currency handling weren't checked against that real need.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
questions.prompt: What makes a take-over rule useful, per lesson two?

options.label: It's specific and checkable — applicable to any given line of code, not a vague intention to be careful
It should cover every part of the change equally
It only needs to exist in the developer's head, not in writing

questions.explanation: "Anything that computes a number in the export gets hand-written" is checkable against any specific line; "be careful with the money parts" isn't. Writing it down is also required — a private decision is easy to abandon under pressure.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
questions.prompt: Why is the moment a change feels finished the riskiest moment for self-review, per lesson three?

options.label: Completion satisfaction is a stronger pull toward a confirming read than an ordinary review moment, since motivation to find problems is lowest exactly when desire to be done is highest
It isn't actually riskier than any other review moment
The code is objectively more likely to be correct by that point, so less review is needed

questions.explanation: This is the teamwork module's confirmation mechanism at its strongest — real desire for the review to come back clean, on top of the baseline bias, is exactly why the full procedure matters most here, not least.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
questions.prompt: Which kind of decision genuinely needs a written defence?

options.label: One where a reasonable, informed person could have chosen differently and might ask why you didn't
Every decision made in the change, without exception
Only decisions that turned out to be mistakes

questions.explanation: Format choices, scope cuts, and take-over-rule calls clear this bar; implementation details with no real alternative, like most variable naming, don't — defending everything equally buries what actually matters.

questions.from: Previous module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: What does the real monthly cost of AI tool use include beyond the headline subscription price?

options.label: Every tool actually used at real usage rates, plus time lost to friction
Nothing — the subscription price is the real cost
Only the most expensive single tool used

questions.explanation: A small, remembered headline number invites treating the tool as close to free, hiding the point where it may no longer clearly be worth it.

questions.from: Previous module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: What are the three failure modes worth planning a specific fallback for?

options.label: Full outage, rate limit, and degraded response
Only full outages
Slow internet, typos, and browser crashes

questions.explanation: Each has a genuinely different signature and right response — waiting is often fine for a rate limit and usually wrong for a full outage against a fixed deadline.

questions.from: Previous module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: Which skills does the module say are worth actively maintaining?

options.label: Skills needed at exactly the moment a tool might fail, and skills underlying judgment a tool can't substitute for
Every skill a tool currently handles
Only rarely-used syntax and CLI flags

questions.explanation: Atrophy tracks with what's routinely delegated — debugging under pressure and core architectural judgment clear the bar; pure syntax lookup doesn't.

questions.from: Previous module — Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
questions.prompt: What's the honest comparison between local and hosted AI models?

options.label: Local trades some capability, especially on hard reasoning tasks, for real independence and data control, at a real setup and maintenance cost
Local is strictly worse in every respect
Local is free and has no meaningful capability gap

questions.explanation: Neither extreme is honest — the real tradeoff depends on the specific workload, weighed against the specific capability gap and the specific independence gain.

questions.from: Earlier in the phase — Estimating and Scoping
questions.prompt: What two variables move review time independently of how much code exists?

options.label: Familiarity with the code, and what it costs if it's wrong
Typing speed and lines of code
Programming language and time of day

questions.explanation: This is the exact test the capstone's planning lesson reused to decide the take-over rule.

questions.from: Earlier in the phase — Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What makes a disclosure note real rather than theatre?

options.label: It's specific to the change — removing it would cost the reader real information
It mentions AI use somewhere in the text
It appears identically on every PR

questions.explanation: This is the same test applied to the capstone's disclosure note and to its closing "another week" account — a generic sentence fails it regardless of how true it is in general.

contentSections.body: This closes the phase. Everything here has pulled from every module before it — which is the point: none of this was ever separate skills, just one practice applied at different points in a real piece of work.
